## Goal

This is the book's first dedicated interiority chapter, and it arrives at the right moment: the eve of the gate, when action is suspended and thought is the only available work. The chapter must be anchored to a physical task (building the data packet) and to a physical object (the terminal's cursor, the tape housing in the hut) so that the interiority does not become abstract. Elena is a scientist who thinks through her hands; even when she is thinking, she is holding something.

The chapter is short because the compression is the point. Elena does not have a lot of words for this. Neither does the chapter.

---

## Obstacle

The obstacle is entirely interior: Elena has all the information she needs to decide, and she cannot decide. Not because she lacks information but because neither option closes cleanly. She is spending this chapter doing the one thing her career has not prepared her for: sitting with an unresolved question that will resolve itself whether she acts or not.

---

## Action Beats

1. **Elena does not run the protocol today.** She knows this. She decided it last night, implicitly. She goes to the receiver hut only to check the tape housing temperature (within range) and to look at the tape without touching it. She notes, by examining the reel against the timing marks on the housing, that the edge binder stress has extended. She estimates the affected zone by eye: what was five seconds two days ago is now approximately eight seconds. She does not run the protocol to measure it precisely. She cannot afford the power. She notes "~8s dropout, visual estimate" in the log.

2. **She goes to the fax terminal.** She has done this before — used the terminal for routine maintenance data transmissions when the relay window was active. The terminal's interface is familiar: a text input field, a packet-formatting utility, a status indicator for the relay carrier signal.

3. **She builds the data packet.** This is a concrete, physical task. She formats the signal's compressed metadata according to the USAP data transmission protocol: frequency band, timestamp, duration, amplitude profile header, the first parametric segment summary (the only complete one; the second segment is still intact at this point but the first is now partially dropout-affected, which she documents). She adds her chain-of-custody notes, her verification protocol summary from Runs 1-3, and a cover statement that she writes and rewrites twice before settling on a version.

4. **The cover statement** (the reader sees Elena writing it, not the text itself). She is aware that this cover statement, if transmitted, will be the first document anyone outside Winslow sees. It will frame what they look at before they look at the data. She has spent her career arguing that the frame matters as much as the content. She writes it. She reads it back to herself. She changes two phrases.

5. **The data packet is complete.** The cursor is blinking. The packet is formatted, addressed to the USAP relay buffer, waiting for the initiation command that will transmit it when the window opens. She has not initiated it. She is looking at the cursor.

6. **She leaves the terminal.** She puts on her outer layer and goes to the receiver hut. She checks the tape housing one more time. She reads through her analysis notebook from Run 1 to Run 3. She sits in the work chair in the cold hut for a while.

7. **The interiority.** (Not labeled as such in the prose; rendered through free indirect interiority in Elena's scientific vocabulary.) She thinks about what it means to send this: the agencies will receive a compressed data packet from a scientist they trust. They will ask for the instrument logs. They will want the tape. They will schedule a verification run using equipment she does not have here — on the assumption that the tape can be transported and the signal analyzed again. She will be the source, not the author. She knows what that means; she has watched it happen to others.

8. She thinks about what it means not to send: she will have three runs and a degrading tape and five days and no institutional channel. She will have to hand it to Walczak on Day 12 with no preparation, no framing, no ability to control what happens next.

9. She thinks about Lars. His reading, filed as noise, sixty kilometers east. She does not pick up the radio.

10. **End of chapter.** She goes back to the equipment building. The data packet is still on the terminal screen. She does not delete it. She does not initiate it. She goes to the hab and lies down on her bunk, which is not sleeping. The cursor is blinking at the unattended terminal. The window opens in less than twelve hours.

---

## Outcome / Elliptical

The chapter ends on the cursor and the absence of a decision. It is deliberately unresolved — not as a technique for suspense but because this is where Elena actually is. She has done everything required to send the data except send it. She has not decided not to send it either. Both options are still open. The window will open regardless.

---

## New Question / Pressure Raised

What will she do when the window opens tomorrow morning?

---

## Craft Notes for the Drafter

- This chapter must be anchored to the **physical act of building the data packet** throughout; if Elena floats free of the task, the interiority becomes abstract and violates the style guidance.
- The cover statement she writes: the reader should sense its weight without seeing its content. The signal's content is never described; the cover statement covers a signal, not a message.
- **Do not resolve the decision in this chapter.** The elliptical ending is structural, not a failure of commitment. Elena is genuinely undecided; the prose must be undecided with her.
- **Do not use this chapter to editorialize on the ethics.** Both options must feel real and costly, not one obviously right and one obviously wrong.

---

## Continuity Notes

- Tape dropout: now visually estimated at ~8 seconds (up from 5 seconds on Day 4). This estimate will be confirmed when Chapter 9 (Run 4) measures the dropout more precisely; the slight discrepancy between Elena's visual estimate and the instrument's measurement is realistic.
- Power reserve: ~47 % after this chapter. No instrument run today.
- Hours to gate: under 24 h at chapter's end.
- The **data packet** built in this chapter is a canonical document: it is formatted, addressed, and sitting on the terminal's send queue. Whether it is transmitted (Chapter 7) or not is the gate chapter's question. The data packet's existence is established here.

# Chapter 07 — The Window

**One-line summary:** The relay window opens at 0800 and closes at 0848; Elena does not transmit; the institutional channel closes permanently.

**POV:** Dr. Elena Hartmann  
**Tense:** Third-person limited past  
**Setting:** Winslow Station — receiver hut, fax terminal (equipment building), back to receiver hut. Day 7, 0500–0848.  
**Target words:** ~3,100  
**Chapter shape:** Bottle — single time-compressed sequence, near real-time from pre-dawn to 0848  
**Ending mode:** Mid-action cut

---

## Escalation (from Chapter Map)

- **(a) Day 7, 0800–0848**
- **(b)** Hours to gate: 0. Days to foreclosure: 5 (new operative quantity). Power reserve: 47 % → 41 % (terminal active during window + warm-up cycles).
- **(c)** **PERMANENTLY FORECLOSED:** the institutional relay transmission channel. The window will not recur before Day 12. Elena now holds the data and must decide what to do with it in five days.

---

## Goal

This is the book's hardest chapter and its structural hinge. The relay window opens and closes. Something is decided — by action or by inaction, both are choices — and after this chapter, the path not taken is gone. The chapter must be long because it is the book's pivot; because the forty-eight minutes of the window must be felt; because Elena's non-transmission must be shown, not told, without any suggestion that the decision was made before this moment.

**The decision must be genuine until it is done.** The drafter must not signal, foreshadow, or retroactively imply that Elena "knew all along" she wouldn't send. She is in the room, she has the data packet on the terminal, the carrier signal is live, and she is choosing. The chapter ends at the moment the carrier dies, not in Elena's reflection about the choice.

---

## Obstacle

Time. The window is 48 minutes. Every minute of inaction is a minute of decision. And: the tape shows new degradation (eight-second dropout measured this morning before the window), which could push her toward sending — or toward realizing the tape is dying and she needs to verify once more before she commits to a transmission that frames the data without its last clean verification.

---

## Action Beats

**0500–0700: Pre-dawn**

1. Elena wakes before she intends to. She is not rested. She makes coffee in the galley, standing at the cold stove. The mug warms more slowly than it should because the corridor hatch seal is cracked.

2. She goes to the receiver hut at 0530, an hour and a half before the window. She checks the tape. She holds the housing and looks at the reel through its inspection panel. She takes out the timing-mark tool and measures the dropout against the marks: eight seconds confirmed, maybe eight and a half. It has grown overnight.

3. She does not run the protocol. She cannot — the power reserve is at 47 %, and a stabilization procedure plus a protocol run before the window would push the reserve low enough that the terminal draw during the window would risk a brownout. She has to choose between a run and a clean transmission window. She chooses the clean window.

4. She returns to the equipment building. The fax terminal screen is dark (sleep mode). She wakes it. The data packet is still there — she did not close it last night. The cursor blinks.

5. She reads through the cover statement again. She makes one small change to a phrase. The change is not improvement; it is postponement.

6. **0630.** She sits at the terminal and reads through the data packet's metadata summary. She is not checking it for errors; she checked it yesterday. She is reading it the way you read a document you have already decided to sign.

**0700–0800: The hour before the window**

7. The relay carrier signal indicator on the terminal is dark. The window has not opened. She checks the clock.

8. She goes to the receiver hut again. She stands in front of the signal analyzer and looks at the amber numerals of the analyzer's standby display. She thinks about the signal as it arrived — the moment on Day 1 when the numerals changed. She thinks about what the data packet's compressed metadata will look like in the USAP relay buffer, eight hours from now, in McMurdo.

9. She thinks about who will read it first. Someone in the McMurdo operations center, passing it up the chain. The chain is not abstract to Elena; she knows the chain. She knows the names, the institutional dynamics, the grant structures. She knows what happens when a signal of this kind moves through those structures without a scientist's hand on it.

10. She checks the clock again: 0750.

11. She returns to the terminal. She sits down.

**0800–0848: The window**

12. **0800.** The carrier signal indicator on the terminal flashes green. The relay satellite has come over the horizon; the uplink window is open. She has 48 minutes.

13. She does not move immediately. She looks at the indicator. The terminal is showing the packet queue: one item, addressed and ready. The initiation command is a single keystroke.

14. She picks up a pen and writes a timestamp in her notebook: "0800 — window open." She does not know why she is doing this; it is the action of someone who needs something to do with her hands.

15. **0812.** She is still sitting at the terminal. The cursor blinks. She has used twelve minutes.

16. She stands. She goes to the equipment building's small window — the only exterior window in the building — and looks out at the Antarctic dark. She can see nothing. She comes back to the terminal.

17. **0822.** She has the initiation command ready. She does not execute it.

18. She leaves the terminal and goes, one more time, to the receiver hut. This is not analysis. This is the kind of movement that happens when a body cannot sit still at the moment it most needs to sit still.

19. In the receiver hut: the tape housing, the analyzer, the printout gone to the hab cabinet. She puts her hand on the tape housing. She is thinking about Lars, about the data filed as noise at Mather. If she transmits, the agencies will have one record — hers, partially dropout-affected, with a degrading second parametric segment. If she holds, she has three runs and five days, and the tape will degrade further, and on Day 12 the choice is different but not better.

20. **0838.** She returns to the terminal.

21. She sits down. The window closes in ten minutes.

22. She reads the cover statement one final time. She has not changed anything. Her hand is near the keyboard.

23. **0848.** The carrier signal indicator goes dark. The satellite has moved past the transmission window. The indicator shows: CARRIER LOST.

24. The data packet is still on the terminal. The window is gone.

25. Elena sits for a long moment. Her hand is no longer near the keyboard. The packet queue shows: one item, unsent.

---

## Outcome / Mid-Action Cut

**End chapter here — at the carrier loss, not after.**

The mid-action cut lands at 0848 when the CARRIER LOST indicator appears. The drafter must not write Elena's reflection, her relief or regret, or any naming of what she has done. The chapter's last beat is the indicator going dark, full stop. The aftermath is Chapter 8's work.

---

## New Question / Pressure Raised

She has five days. She has three runs. She has a degrading tape. She chose not to send — or she did not choose to send, which is not the same thing, though it has the same result. What does she do now?

---

## Craft Notes for the Drafter

- The 48-minute window must be **felt as 48 minutes**, not summarized. Use the timestamps. Let the chapter breathe around them. The elapsed time is the chapter's mechanism.
- The **decision must be genuine throughout.** The reader should believe until 0848 that Elena might send. She might have. She didn't. Both must be true simultaneously.
- The **mid-action cut** on the carrier-loss indicator is the chapter's ending. No reaction. No summary. No Elena's face, her hands, her breathing, her thought. The carrier dies; the chapter ends. This is the only acceptable ending mode for this chapter.
- Physical movement through the chapter — terminal to receiver hut to window to terminal — is expressive of Elena's inability to sit still at the moment of decision. But the movements should not be so numerous that they begin to feel like stalling; they should feel like the way a careful person paces before an irreversible act.
- Do not use "she decided" at any point in this chapter. The prose must show the decision happening (or not happening) without naming it.

---

## Continuity Notes

- **The institutional relay transmission option is permanently foreclosed after this chapter.** This is a hard continuity fact. The next relay window does not occur before Day 12; the LC-130 is the only remaining channel. No subsequent chapter may introduce an alternative uplink mechanism.
- The tape dropout is **eight seconds** at the start of this chapter (confirmed from Chapter 6's visual estimate; no Run 3 was done today). This will next be measured precisely in Chapter 9 (Run 4, Day 8), where it will have grown to twelve seconds in the core record.
- Power reserve: ~41 % after this chapter (terminal draw during the 48-minute window + building warm-up).
- Days to foreclosure: 5 (operative quantity from this chapter forward; replaces "hours to gate").
- Instrument run margin: still 3 remaining (no run done in this chapter).

# Chapter 08 — After

**One-line summary:** Post-gate reckoning; generator fault forces Elena outside; she stands in the Antarctic dark and calculates what she now holds and what she must do with it.

**POV:** Dr. Elena Hartmann  
**Tense:** Third-person limited past  
**Setting:** Winslow Station — main hab (galley), equipment building (generator), exterior, back to main hab. Day 7, afternoon and evening.  
**Target words:** ~2,000  
**Chapter shape:** Interiority-heavy — second of the two permitted interiority chapters; anchored to the generator fault response and the exterior walk  
**Ending mode:** Literary fade

---

## Escalation (from Chapter Map)

- **(a) Day 7, afternoon/evening**
- **(b)** Generator fault: voltage variance widens (generator drops to ~90 % output; manual stabilization required for the first time). Tape dropout: eight seconds confirmed on visual recheck during power reduction. Power reserve: 41 % → 38 %. Days to foreclosure: 5.
- **(c)** Step closer: Elena calculates the new arithmetic — 3 runs, 5 days, degrading tape — and recognizes she has no escape mechanism remaining. The exits now are: hand the data to the team on Day 12, destroy it, or pursue some form of publication she has no mechanism to execute from here. She must choose among outcomes, not among options.

---

## Goal

The aftermath chapter. What does it feel like to have let the gate close? Not relief — the brief says that extra time must read as pressure, never relief. The chapter's job is to show Elena understanding the new pressure regime: the institutional option is gone, the tape is worse than yesterday, the power is lower, and she has five days in which the choice about Day 12 must crystallize. The anchor is the generator fault — a physical crisis that forces her outside into the Antarctic winter, which is the only time in the novel she is fully exposed to the cold and the dark.

---

## Obstacle

The generator fault is the immediate obstacle: it is not catastrophic but it requires attention, and the procedure for stabilizing it (load-shedding the heater, allowing the generator to normalize without load, then restoring the heater draw) takes forty-five minutes during which the hut will get colder. After she stabilizes it, she must go outside to check the generator exhaust — a routine check made more urgent by the fault — which puts her in the full winter dark at minus-forty.

---

## Action Beats

**Afternoon**

1. Elena has not eaten since before the window. She makes something in the galley — the mechanical action of a person who has learned to maintain function when function is what you have. She stands at the counter and eats without sitting down.

2. She does not know what she is thinking. That is the opening condition of this chapter: not numbness, not grief, but the strange clarity of having passed a point and not yet arrived at the next one.

3. The generator alarm: a low-frequency fault tone from the equipment building, which Elena has heard twice before (minor voltage excursions, both resolved on their own). This one does not resolve on its own. She goes.

4. In the equipment building: the generator's output display is reading 89 % and fluctuating. The voltage regulator fault light is active. She runs the stabilization procedure: identifies the highest-draw circuit (the receiver hut's heater), sheds it, waits for the generator to normalize at reduced load. The procedure takes forty minutes.

5. During those forty minutes, Elena sits on the equipment-building bench with the generator's hum and watches the output gauge. It is the closest thing to quiet that this chapter has.

6. What she thinks about while she waits: not the decision she has made (she does not name it to herself as a decision in this chapter), but the arithmetic of what remains. Three runs. Five days. A tape degrading at roughly one second per day (her current estimate, which will prove slightly optimistic). In five days, the dropout may be at thirteen seconds. Which means: if she runs on Day 8, Day 10, and Day 12, she will have snapshots of the tape's deterioration — but each run also risks a brownout, and the power reserve is now at 38 %.

7. The generator stabilizes. She restores the heater draw. She makes a log entry: "Day 7 afternoon: generator fault, voltage regulator active fault. Stabilization procedure executed. Duration: 40 min. No instruments lost."

**Exterior**

8. She needs to check the generator exhaust pipe — a standard post-fault check to make sure the pipe hasn't partially iced. This requires going outside. She dresses for it: full cold-weather kit, which takes seven minutes to put on correctly. She has learned not to rush this.

9. Outside. The temperature: minus forty-two Celsius. No wind at this moment, which is rarer than it sounds. The sky — when she looks up — is the thing she always forgets to prepare for: not black but a texture of stars so dense they appear as a material, as if the sky were a surface rather than a depth.

10. She is outside for perhaps five minutes. She checks the exhaust: no icing. She stands for a moment that is longer than it needs to be.

11. **The calculation, outside.** She does it while she can see the stars. What she is not going to do: send the data up a channel that doesn't exist anymore. What she has not yet decided: what she is going to do instead. Destroy it — the thought is present, not as a plan but as a door that exists in the same space as the other doors. Hand it to Walczak with no framing — another door. Write it up herself, which requires resources she doesn't have and a publication window she doesn't have from here. Lars — the thought of Lars arrives and leaves quickly. There is something there. She doesn't follow it.

12. She goes back inside.

**Evening**

13. Back in the equipment building. She takes off the cold-weather kit. She goes to the galley and makes tea. The mug cools faster than usual because she is not paying attention to it.

14. She does not delete the data packet from the terminal. She does not open it. She goes to the receiver hut for a brief check of the tape housing — still within range, the heater working again. She does not touch the tape.

15. **End of chapter.** She is in the galley with the tea going cold and the SSB radio's red standby light glowing in the dark. She has not made a decision. She has made a calculation. The two are different things, and she knows which one she has done.

---

## Outcome / Literary Fade

The literary fade: the galley at evening, the red standby light, the tea cooling, Elena sitting without moving. The chapter ends before she moves again. The pressure is present in the stillness — not the peace of resolution but the particular weight of a person at the end of Day 7 who has foreclosed one option and not yet named another.

---

## New Question / Pressure Raised

Three runs. Five days. A degrading tape. Lars's data at Mather. The data packet still on the terminal. Day 12 coming. What is she going to do?

---

## Craft Notes for the Drafter

- This is the second interiority chapter. It must be **anchored to the generator fault and the exterior walk** — Elena does not simply sit and think; she is working, then briefly outside, then returning. The thinking happens inside the physical work.
- The exterior scene is the **only time in the novel Elena is fully exposed to the Antarctic winter exterior.** It should carry that weight — but without becoming metaphorical. The stars are not a metaphor. The cold is not a symbol. They are the precise physical condition of being outside at Winslow Station in June 1991 at minus forty-two.
- **Do not name Elena's relief or regret** about the gate passing. Neither word should appear in this chapter, and neither concept should be explained by the narration. What Elena feels is present in the physical detail of how she moves through the chapter.
- The thought about **Lars** in Beat 11 is brief and does not resolve. It seeds Chapter 10's revelation without telegraphing it. One or two sentences, then she doesn't follow the thread.

---

## Continuity Notes

- This chapter is **Day 7, afternoon and evening** — same calendar day as Chapter 7. Days to foreclosure: still 5 (since the gate closing is what reset the clock, and the clock resets to 5 at 0848 Day 7).
- Tape dropout: eight seconds (confirmed visually during the generator fault response, when the heater was briefly offline and she checked the housing). This will be measured more precisely in Chapter 9 as twelve seconds in the core record — the visual estimate was of the edge dropout; the core dropout began later and is worse than the edge suggests.
- Power reserve: ~38 % after this chapter.
- Instrument run margin: still 3 remaining.
- The data packet from Chapter 6 is still on the fax terminal, unsent. Its existence is not mentioned explicitly in this chapter unless it arises naturally; it is a background fact.

# Chapter 09 — Core Dropout

**One-line summary:** Protocol Run 4 reveals a twelve-second dropout in the second parametric segment; full parametric verification is permanently foreclosed; what remains is the first segment and the core signature.

**POV:** Dr. Elena Hartmann  
**Tense:** Third-person limited past  
**Setting:** Winslow Station — receiver hut (Run 4), then main hab (analysis). Day 8.  
**Target words:** ~2,800  
**Chapter shape:** Single scene — one extended activity (Protocol Run 4 and its aftermath)  
**Ending mode:** Turn

---

## Escalation (from Chapter Map)

- **(a) Day 8**
- **(b)** Tape integrity: Run 4 reveals a **twelve-second dropout in the core record** — the second parametric segment is gone. The dropout is no longer edge-only. Instrument run margin: 3 → 2. Power reserve: 38 % → 30 %. Days to foreclosure: 4.
- **(c)** **PERMANENTLY FORECLOSED:** full parametric verification. The complete parameter set Elena's protocol was designed to prove is no longer achievable with this tape. What remains is the first parametric segment (minus its opening five-to-eight seconds, now lost) and the core signature — sufficient for a provisional claim but not a peer-reviewed one.

---

## Goal

Deliver the chapter's turn cleanly: the tape is worse than Elena's visual estimates indicated, and the damage is now in the part of the record that matters most for the precision of her claim. This chapter is about what it costs to have a career founded on the standard of proof she insisted on — and to discover that the instrument is now definitively below that standard. What remains is still real. It is just not what she built her career to produce.

---

## Obstacle

The stabilization procedure required before the run (due to the widened voltage variance after yesterday's fault) costs fifteen minutes of generator draw. Elena cannot skip it. She has learned from the chapter 8 fault that the voltage variance is widening; running the instrument without stabilization would risk data corruption in the run, making it worse than not running at all.

---

## Action Beats

**Preparation**

1. Elena wakes on Day 8 with a clear intention: she will run the protocol today. She has not run it since Day 4. The tape has been degrading for four days in between. She needs to know the current state.

2. The stabilization procedure: she runs the generator at reduced instrument load for fifteen minutes before starting the analyzer, letting the voltage variance settle. She watches the output gauge. The variance is wider than it was before Day 7's fault — running at +/- 7 % instead of the +/- 5 % she had before. Not catastrophic, but she notes it.

3. She checks the tape housing temperature. Within range. She takes the reel out of the housing and does a brief visual inspection before the run: the binder stress zone is visibly larger than Day 4, though still concentrated at the reel edge.

**Protocol Run 4**

4. She initiates Run 4. The warm-up cycle. The analyzer's amber numerals cycling through their self-test. The tape loads into the playback head.

5. **First parametric segment.** The tape plays. She watches the analyzer's output display as the frequency sweep runs through the first parametric segment. The opening five to eight seconds: silence. The binder failure she documented in Chapter 4, now slightly wider. Then: the rest of the first segment plays cleanly. The frequency distribution is intact. The first parametric profile reads.

6. **The gap.** Between the first and second parametric segments, there is a brief silence that is normal — a transition in the signal's structure. She knows this part of the recording; she has run this protocol three times before. The transition ends and the second parametric segment should begin.

7. **It does not begin.** The analyzer's display shows: no signal. Not noise, not degraded signal — silence. She watches for ten seconds. Fifteen. The analyzer is not receiving anything from the tape in this region.

8. She stops the run. Rewinds to the beginning of the second parametric segment. Plays it again. Same result: twelve seconds of silence where the second segment should be, followed — at twelve seconds — by the tape recovering and the signal resuming in the third segment (a shorter calibration tail that is not parametric but confirms the event's duration).

9. She plays the twelve-second gap three times. It is not recoverable. The binder has failed in the core of the record, not just the edge. The second parametric segment — the one that extends and completes the parametric profile, the one that gives the signal's full characterization — is gone.

**Completion of the run**

10. She lets the run complete. Everything after the twelve-second gap reads: the calibration tail, the post-event baseline. The core signature — the structure that makes the signal non-terrestrial and non-natural — is intact in the first parametric segment. That is not nothing. But the full parametric profile her protocol was designed to establish requires both segments, and the second segment is gone.

11. Power reserve after the run: ~30 %. Instrument margin: 2 remaining.

**Analysis**

12. She sits in the work chair with the run log printout in her hand. She goes through it slowly, in the way she has gone through data for thirty years: assuming first that she has made an error, checking each step, eliminating the possibility of error one element at a time.

13. She has not made an error. The second parametric segment is unreadable. The tape binder has failed in the core of the signal record.

14. She goes through what remains: the first parametric segment (minus its opening five-to-eight seconds, now also lost to binder failure) is sufficient to establish the signal as anomalous, non-terrestrial, non-natural. It is not sufficient — alone — for the full parametric characterization her protocol was designed to produce. What she can claim, on this basis, is: a signal was received, its primary anomalous parameters are X, Y, and Z (from the first segment), its duration was forty-seven seconds, it did not repeat. What she cannot claim, on this basis, is the complete parametric profile that would allow a peer reviewer to say: "This is definitively [X category] and not [Y category] within the established classification framework."

15. She writes this down in the analysis notebook. Carefully, in the precise language she would use in a paper. She is not writing a draft of a paper; she is writing an honest accounting of what the evidence now supports and does not support.

16. She takes the run log back to the receiver hut and files it in the protocol folder she has been maintaining since Day 1.

**End of chapter**

17. She stands in the hut for a moment with the folder in her hands. The tape is in its housing. The signal analyzer is back in standby. The amber numerals have gone quiet.

18. What she has: the core signature of the signal, readable in the first parametric segment. The signal's duration and primary anomalous parameters. Her three prior runs confirming the signal's presence. The printout (still intact as of Day 4; she will check it again). The analysis notebook. Two runs remaining.

19. What she does not have: the full parametric profile. The second segment. The chain of evidence that would survive the peer review she had designed her protocol to pass.

---

## Outcome / Turn

The turn recontextualizes everything: Elena spent ten days (in her career) building a protocol that produces a level of proof she can no longer achieve with the tape she has. She can still make a claim. But not the claim she built her career to make. The tape has decided for her what kind of claim this will be.

---

## New Question / Pressure Raised

What kind of claim does the remaining evidence support, and is Elena willing to make it? Is a provisional claim — one that states the signal's primary anomalous parameters without the full profile — something she can stake her name on, given that her name stands for the other thing?

---

## Continuity Notes

- The **twelve-second core dropout in the second parametric segment** is the chapter's hard fact. All subsequent chapters must treat the second parametric segment as unrecoverable.
- The **first parametric segment** (minus its opening five-to-eight seconds) is still readable. The core signature (the structure that makes the signal non-terrestrial and non-natural) is intact. This is the basis for whatever claim Elena ultimately makes.
- The **third segment** (calibration tail) is intact and readable; it confirms the event's forty-seven-second duration.
- Instrument margin: 2 remaining after this chapter. Power reserve: ~30 %.
- Days to foreclosure: 4.
- The voltage variance is now noted as +/- 7 % (widened from +/- 5 % before the Day 7 generator fault). This will worsen further in Chapter 10.

- **(b)** Generator voltage variance: +/- 8 % (was +/- 7 % after Day 7 fault; widening). Each remaining run now requires a pre-run stabilization procedure costing fifteen minutes of generator draw and additional power reserve. Days to foreclosure: 3. Power reserve: 30 % → 24 %.

The option to be the sole holder of knowledge about the signal is foreclosed. But the corroboration is inaccessible as evidence unless Elena tells Lars what he had, which would mean telling Lars.

---

## Goal

Two interlocking discoveries in one chapter: the generator is getting worse (making each remaining run more expensive), and there is corroborating data sixty kilometers away that Elena cannot use without revealing her hand. This chapter is about a form of abundance — corroboration she didn't have yesterday — that cannot actually help her, and may make her situation worse.

---

## Obstacle

The SSB contact with Lars is a scheduled exchange governed by radio protocol. Elena cannot ask directly; she can only listen. What Lars reveals, he reveals because he is being thorough, not because he knows what Elena is sitting on. The harder Lars's revelation is to hear, the more disciplined Elena must be in not responding to it.

---

## Action Beats

**Beat 1: Morning generator assessment**

1. Elena begins Day 9 with the generator check. She has been doing this every morning; today the numbers are worse than yesterday. The voltage variance has widened to +/- 8 % — a significant jump from the +/- 7 % she recorded after the Day 7 fault. The generator is not failing, but it is degrading toward a failure state that the new regulator component (arriving on Day 12 with Walczak) would fix.

2. She runs the math she has been avoiding: if each remaining instrument run now requires a fifteen-minute stabilization procedure to bring the voltage variance into safe range, and the stabilization procedure costs approximately 3–4 % of the power reserve on top of the run itself, then each of her two remaining runs will cost roughly 12–14 % of remaining reserve (stabilization + run draw). At current reserve (~28 % heading into today), she has room for two runs, but barely — and only if nothing else goes wrong.

3. She records the fault data in the maintenance log, in the same columns she has been filling since Day 1. The columns are almost full.

4. She does not run the protocol today. She cannot afford to spend a run without a clear purpose, and today's purpose is the Lars contact.

**Beat 2: SSB contact with Lars Engström**

5. The scheduled contact opens at 1400. Lars identifies by call sign. He is preparing his monthly report to the Norwegian Polar Institute and has been going through his instrument logs more carefully than usual.

6. Routine exchange first: weather (a wind event at Mather, moderate, has passed), station status, Lars's chemistry data. Lars mentions that his data collection has been going well; his winterover work is producing the results he expected.

7. Then Lars says: he went back to look at that anomalous reading he mentioned on Day 3. His monthly report requires him to either document or formally discard anomalous readings, so he has been more careful with it.

8. He gives the parameters. Duration: **forty-seven seconds.** He is precise because he has now timed it from his log trace. Frequency: UHF secondary band (he names the specific frequency). Timestamp: he gives the date and time.

9. Elena asks him to repeat the duration. She keeps her voice level.

10. Lars repeats it: forty-seven seconds. He adds: "The timing precision is a little low — the logging interval on that band is two seconds, so I should say forty-six to forty-eight seconds. But forty-seven is the center."

11. Elena does the calculation in her head. The timestamp Lars has given is fourteen minutes before her own detection at Winslow. The propagation delay from a source at interstellar distance, received first at Mather (which sits sixty kilometers east on a bearing consistent with the sky region Elena was monitoring), and fourteen minutes later at Winslow — it is consistent. Not proof, but consistent.

12. She asks: has he filed this in his formal station log? Lars says: "I've noted it as unresolved instrument artifact. That's all it seems to be — my diagnostics don't flag any instrument fault, but I can't rule out RFI from our maintenance cycle. I'll note it in the monthly report as an unresolved anomaly and move on."

13. Elena says nothing for a moment that is one beat too long for comfortable radio protocol. Then: "What frequency exactly?" Lars gives the precise frequency. She writes it down.

14. She says: "I had something similar here. I think you're right about RFI." This is the first direct lie Elena has told in this chapter. It is the only lie she has told in the novel. She does not make it dramatic; she says it in the same voice she uses for everything on this radio.

15. Lars says: "Good to know it's not just us. Strange month." He signs off.

16. After the radio goes quiet, Elena holds the handset for a moment before setting it down. Lars has the corroborating data. It sits in his log as an unresolved anomaly — documented but not analyzed. If he knew what he was looking at, his record would be independent confirmation: a different station, a different frequency band, a different instrument, an earlier detection time consistent with the propagation geometry.

17. He does not know what he is looking at. She has just told him it is probably RFI.

18. She cannot un-tell him that. She could call back. She could say: "Lars, I need you to look at that reading again." She does not.

19. Days to foreclosure: 3. She writes in the notebook: "Mather Station: 47s event, UHF [frequency], T-14 min relative to Winslow reception. Lars Engström. Filed as unresolved artifact." She stares at what she has written. Then she closes the notebook.

---

## Outcome / Cliffhanger

The cliffhanger is the gap between what the corroboration could do and what Elena can now do with it. She has independent confirmation of the signal from an independent instrument at an independent location — and it is filed as noise in Lars's monthly report, increasingly unusable because she has just told him she thinks it is RFI. The option to deploy this corroboration without revealing everything she has withheld for nine days is effectively closed. Three days to foreclosure.

---

## New Question / Pressure Raised

She has just told Lars it is probably RFI. Can she un-tell him? If she calls back, what does she say? And: does she want the corroboration enough to reveal what she has been sitting on for nine days to the one person who could confirm it?

---

## Escalation (from Chapter Map)

- **(a) Day 10**
- **(b)** Printout integrity: two columns ink-degraded from cold contraction — the timestamp column and the calibration reference column are partially illegible, three specific data points unreadable. Tape dropout: visual measurement confirms 18 seconds (up from 12 seconds at Run 4 two days ago). Days to foreclosure: 2. Power reserve: 24 % → 20 % (passive overnight draw; no run today).
- **(c)** Step closer: the printout's chain-of-custody timestamp is partially illegible. The printout can no longer independently verify the receipt time of the signal without the instrument log to corroborate it. The photograph record (twelve frames, station camera) exists but is not instrument-verifiable.

---

## Goal

A quiet chapter in one sense — no instrument run, no radio contact, no external event — but one that reveals the physical toll of eleven days on the evidence base. The chapter's subject is the artifacts themselves: what they look like, what they show, and what they no longer show. Elena is meticulous and patient; this chapter lets the reader see that patience working on a problem that patience cannot fully fix.

---

## Obstacle

The cold has done what cold does to paper and ink. The printout — which Elena has maintained in the warmest accessible location (the equipment cabinet in the hab) — has still degraded, because the hab is not warm by any habitable standard. The ink on thermal paper at sustained cold temperatures becomes brittle and cracks along the printed lines. She cannot uncrack the ink; she can only document the damage before it gets worse.

---

## Action Beats

**Printout examination (main hab)**

1. Elena retrieves the printout from the equipment cabinet — still in its gray thermal blanket. She takes it to the galley table and unrolls it fully, weighting the corners with objects from the shelf: a can, a tool kit, a book.

2. She examines it column by column under the work light. The printout has fourteen columns: frequency, amplitude, time-of-reception (the timestamp column), phase, polarization, signal-to-noise, calibration reference, and seven derived parameter columns produced by the signal analyzer's processing.

3. The damage: **Column 3 (timestamp)** — the time-of-reception column — shows hairline fractures in the ink along three of its numerical lines. Two of the three timestamps are partially illegible; the third is a complete blank where the ink has flaked. The signal's specific time-of-reception — the number that connects this record to the antenna log and the station's timekeeping — is no longer readable from the printout alone.

4. **Column 7 (calibration reference)** — the column that records the signal analyzer's calibration state at the moment of the run — shows similar fracturing in two of its entries. These are not the signal parameters themselves, but the reference values against which the signal parameters are measured. Without them, the printed parameter values cannot be independently verified as accurate without access to the original instrument log.

5. The twelve remaining columns: intact. The signal's frequency distribution, amplitude profile, phase structure, polarization — these are readable. The core anomalous parameters are present and legible. The damage is not to the signal's characteristics but to the chain-of-custody and calibration data that anchors the printout to verifiable science.

6. Elena makes a note in the analysis notebook: which columns are affected, which entries are degraded, which specific values are unreadable. She writes them as precisely as she can: "Column 3 (timestamp): rows 4, 7 partially degraded; row 12 blank. Column 7 (cal ref): rows 2, 9 degraded."

**Photography**

7. She retrieves the station camera from the equipment building — a 35mm SLR used for site documentation and ice surveys. She has eighteen exposures left on the current roll.

8. She photographs the printout systematically: one frame per column, then three frames of the two damaged columns at close range to capture what remains legible. Twelve frames total. She uses the camera carefully — she knows about cold and camera equipment; the mechanism is slightly stiff from the temperature.

9. The photographs exist now. But photographs of a damaged document are evidence of the damage, not a restoration of the data. They show what is there and what is not; they do not supply the missing values.

**Tape inspection (receiver hut)**

10. She goes to the receiver hut. The tape inspection she does not run with the instrument — she measures the dropout manually against the timing marks on the housing, as she has been doing when she cannot afford a full run. The affected zone has grown since Run 4's twelve seconds. By her measurement: **eighteen seconds.** The binder failure is spreading toward the center of the reel.

11. She documents the visual state of the tape surface at the dropout zone: the binder has flaked completely in a narrow band, revealing the underlying tape substrate. The flaking is stable — it is not generating loose debris — but the zone of failure is now wider than the signal's second parametric segment, which is gone, and is beginning to approach the boundary of the core signature region.

12. She calculates: if the dropout grows at a consistent rate of three seconds per day (from the progression she has measured: 5s on Day 4, 8s estimated Day 6, 12s confirmed Day 8, 18s estimated Day 10), the dropout will reach the edge of the core signature region in approximately two to three days. The core signature is not gone yet. But it is the next thing to go if the degradation continues.

13. She considers running a protocol run now — but the power reserve is at 22 % and the instrument run would cost approximately 10–12 % including the stabilization procedure. She decides to hold the remaining two runs for Days 11 and 12.

**Return to hab**

14. She re-rolls the printout carefully and rewraps it in the thermal blanket. She puts it back in the equipment cabinet. She looks at the stack of photographs — exposed, not yet developed (no darkroom at Winslow; the film will go to McMurdo for development when the team arrives).

15. **End of chapter.** She makes her log entry for Day 10: "Printout: Col 3, Col 7 partial degradation. Photographs taken (12 frames). Tape: visual dropout estimate 18s. No instrument run. Power reserve estimate 20%." She puts the notebook away. She does not make tea. She sits in the quiet hab with the red standby light of the SSB radio.

---

## Outcome / Literary Fade

The literary fade: Elena wrapping the printout in the thermal blanket, the station quiet, the red standby light. The chapter ends with everything documented and nothing fixed. The physical record exists; it is smaller than it was yesterday.

---

## New Question / Pressure Raised

The core signature is two to three days from the dropout's leading edge. Will it survive through the two remaining runs? And: if the printout's timestamp is unreadable, how does Elena establish when the signal was received without recourse to the instrument log — which requires the signal analyzer to verify?

---

# Chapter 12 — One Remaining

**One-line summary:** Protocol Run 5 confirms the dropout at twenty seconds and defines the final state of the evidence; one instrument run remains; Elena writes the complete evidence summary in her analysis notebook.

**POV:** Dr. Elena Hartmann

**Target words:** ~2,800  
**Chapter shape:** Single scene — one extended activity (Protocol Run 5 and the analysis that follows it)  
**Ending mode:** Resolved beat

---

## Escalation (from Chapter Map)

- **(a) Day 11, morning**
- **(b)** Tape dropout: confirmed at **20 seconds** by instrument (Run 5; more precise than visual estimate of 18 on Day 10). Instrument run margin: 2 → 1. Power reserve: 20 % → 13 %. Days to foreclosure: 1 (the LC-130 arrives tomorrow).
- **(c)** Step closer: with one run remaining and one day left, Elena writes the complete evidence summary in her analysis notebook — what she has, what she no longer has, what can be claimed. The evidence is fixed. It will not improve. She must decide how to present this to Walczak.

---

## Goal

The chapter's resolved beat is the moment Elena finishes the evidence summary in her notebook — not relief, not satisfaction, but the particular weight of knowing the reckoning is complete. She knows exactly what she has. The knowing is the resolution; it does not resolve what she does with what she knows.

---

## Obstacle

The generator's voltage variance at +/- 8 % means the stabilization procedure before the run is not optional. She must burn fifteen minutes and additional reserve before she can start. The stabilization might not hold — a fault during the run would corrupt the data. She runs anyway because she needs to know the current state of the tape before tomorrow.

---

## Action Beats

**Stabilization procedure**

1. Elena wakes on Day 11 with a clear agenda. She has one day before the LC-130. She needs to know the tape's current state before she decides anything about tomorrow. She will run the protocol this morning.

2. She goes to the equipment building for the stabilization procedure. The morning voltage variance: she checks the fault log — five additional minor excursions overnight. The variance is at +/- 8 %, same as yesterday. She runs the stabilization: heater shed, reduced instrument load, fifteen minutes. She watches the gauge. The variance settles to +/- 5 % under reduced load. Good enough.

3. She restores the instrument load slowly. The variance holds. She initiates the run sequence.

**Protocol Run 5**

4. The run begins. The warm-up cycle: familiar, steady. The tape loads. Elena watches the analyzer's output.

5. **Opening segment:** The beginning of the signal — the calibration lead and the start of the first parametric segment. The opening seconds are silence: the binder failure at the reel edge. She measures it mentally against the timing: she estimates it at seven or eight seconds. Slightly worse than the eight she had on Day 7.

6. **First parametric segment (body):** Still intact. The frequency distribution reads cleanly. The primary anomalous parameters — the ones that make the signal non-terrestrial and non-natural — are present. She does not let herself feel anything about this yet; she is watching the display, not interpreting.

7. **Gap:** The twelve-second silence at the transition to the second parametric segment. Same as Run 4. The second segment begins at twelve seconds: silence. Elena notes it. The instrument's precise measurement: **twenty seconds** of silence across the gap (from the start of the expected second segment to the point where the calibration tail begins). This is two seconds more than the twelve seconds she measured at Run 4 two days ago. The dropout is growing: from 12 on Day 8 to 20 on Day 11, approximately 2.7 seconds per day.

8. At that rate: the core signature region — the first parametric segment's body — will be reached by the dropout in approximately four to five days. It will not be reached by tomorrow. The core signature will survive through tomorrow's final run.

9. **Calibration tail:** Intact. Forty-seven-second duration confirmed.

10. **Run complete.** Power reserve: ~13 %. Instrument margin: 1 remaining.

**The evidence summary**

11. Elena goes to the main hab. She makes tea, not because she wants it but because her hands need something to do. She brings her analysis notebook to the galley table and opens it to a blank page.

12. She writes the evidence summary. She takes her time. This is the most important document in the station; she writes it in the language she would use in a paper, not in shorthand. The summary covers:

    - **What exists:** the magnetic tape (physical condition as of Day 11: dropout at 20s, core signature intact); the printout (physical condition: two columns partially degraded, core parameter columns intact); the analysis notebook (this document); twelve photographic frames (not yet developed); instrument run logs for Runs 1–5.
    - **What the instrument runs established:** the signal's duration (47 seconds), primary anomalous parameters (from the first parametric segment), confirmation of non-terrestrial and non-natural character of the signal pattern. What the runs have NOT established: the complete parametric profile (second segment lost to binder failure as of Run 4).
    - **What the corroborating data shows:** Mather Station (Lars Engström), forty-seven-second event in UHF secondary band, received fourteen minutes before Winslow's detection. Filed as unresolved artifact. Not independently verified; not yet communicable without revealing the signal's existence to Engström.
    - **What can be claimed:** a provisional statement that a signal of specific anomalous character was received for forty-seven seconds on [date/time] at Winslow Station; the primary anomalous parameters; the absence of terrestrial or natural explanation within the scope of the verification protocol; corroborating data at Mather Station (unverified, requires follow-up). What cannot be claimed: a peer-reviewed complete parametric characterization from this tape.
    - **What one additional run (Run 6) can do:** confirm the current state of the tape and the core signature's continued readability, and produce one final verification of the primary anomalous parameters before the chain of custody passes.

13. She reads the summary back to herself, paragraph by paragraph. She makes two small corrections. She does not add or remove any assessments. The summary is honest.

14. She closes the notebook. She puts it with the tape and the printout in the equipment cabinet.

15. **One run remaining.** Tomorrow: the LC-130 arrives at approximately 1300. She has the morning.

---

## Outcome / Resolved Beat

The resolved beat: the evidence summary is complete. Elena knows exactly what she has and what she has lost. She knows what she can claim and what she cannot. The knowing does not resolve what she does tomorrow, but the ambiguity about the evidence is over. This is what there is. It is less than she planned for and more than nothing.

---

## New Question / Pressure Raised

She has one run left, and the core signature will survive through tomorrow morning. She can use the run to produce a final verification. After that, instrument margin is zero. What does she do when Walczak walks in?

The power reserve is at 10 % entering this chapter. The stabilization procedure for the generator's voltage variance and the run itself will bring it to approximately 3 % — barely above life-support threshold. If the stabilization fails to hold and she has a brownout during the run, she will have used her last margin on a corrupt run. She runs it anyway.

---

## Action Beats

**0530: Pre-run**

1. Elena is awake at 0530. She has not slept more than a few hours. She stands in the galley in the partial dark — the station's interior lights on their winter-night setting, amber and low. The page she set aside last night is still on the table, face down. She does not turn it over.

2. She makes coffee. She is aware that this is the last morning she is the only person in this station. In six hours, the hab will have other people in it, with their voices and their equipment and their clean sight lines on everything she has been doing.

3. She brings the tape housing from the equipment cabinet and carries it to the receiver hut. The walkway between them is at its coldest of the morning — the exterior temperature is below minus forty. She can feel the walkway flexing slightly under the wind load.

4. She sets the housing down and runs the space heater in the receiver hut for ten minutes to bring the instrument above operating temperature. She watches the thermometer.

**Stabilization procedure**

5. She goes to the equipment building for the stabilization procedure. The generator's morning fault log: six overnight excursions. The variance is at +/- 9 % at the cold start. Worse than yesterday. She runs the stabilization: heater load shed, generator settling at reduced draw. The variance drops slowly — it takes twenty-two minutes this time, not fifteen. She is patient.

6. At +/- 5.5 % — not as clean as she has had it, but within the acceptable range for a run — she restores the instrument load. She watches for a further excursion. The generator holds.

7. Power reserve after stabilization: ~7 %. The run itself will cost another 4–5 %. She will be at approximately 2–3 % afterward. This is enough to sustain life support and the hab heater through the team's arrival at 1300. It is not a margin she would have chosen to operate within.

**Protocol Run 6**

8. She initiates the run. The last time. The analyzer's warm-up cycle. The tape loads.

9. **Opening segment:** silence at the top — now approximately seven to eight seconds, consistent with the progression she has been tracking. The same silence she has heard in every run since Run 3. It is familiar now, the way the opening gap of a record you've played many times becomes part of the music.

10. **First parametric segment:** the signal reads. The frequency distribution is intact. The primary anomalous parameters — the ones that are the reason for all of this — are present and unchanged. The signal is still there.

11. Elena sits very still while this part of the run plays. She has heard it five times. It is the same every time. The signal does not change because tapes degrade; the signal is preserved in what the binder has not yet taken. This is what she has.

12. **The gap:** twenty-three seconds this time, by the analyzer's measurement. The second parametric segment: gone, same as in Run 4 and Run 5. The calibration tail: intact. Forty-seven seconds total. End of signal.

13. **Run complete.** The analyzer's display settles to its post-run idle state. Instrument margin: 0.

14. Power reserve: ~3 %.

**After the run**

15. Elena sits in the work chair for a moment. She looks at the run log as it prints out — the last protocol log she will produce at this instrument, at this station, in this role. She pulls the log from the printer and holds it.

16. She writes in the analysis notebook: "Run 6 complete. Day 12, 0640. Dropout: 23s (consistent with progression). Core signature: intact. First parametric segment: complete. Second parametric segment: absent (as of Run 4). Instrument margin: 0. Power reserve: approximately 3%. This is the final run."

17. She closes the signal analyzer. She files the run log in the protocol folder. She puts the folder with the tape housing, the wrapped printout, and the analysis notebook. She carries all of it — the full evidence package — to the main hab and puts it on the equipment cabinet.

18. She picks up the face-down page from the table. She reads it — the reader does not see what it says. She folds it once and puts it in the analysis notebook between the last used page and the back cover.

**The handset**

19. She goes to the equipment building and sits at the SSB radio console. She picks up the handset. The radio is on standby; the red indicator light shifts as she warms it up for transmission.

20. The chapter ends here.

---

## Outcome / Mid-Action Cut

**End the chapter on the handset, before any transmission.** The reader does not know who she is calling — McMurdo Ops, Lars Engström, or initiating a broadcast that will reach somewhere — or what she is going to say. The cut is precise: she has the handset, the radio is warm, and the chapter ends.

---

## New Question / Pressure Raised

Who is she calling? What is she going to say? The LC-130 is five hours out.

---

## Craft Notes for the Drafter

- The **mid-action cut** is the chapter's structural requirement. Do not allow Elena to speak into the radio in this chapter. Do not allow her to dial or key the transmitter. The chapter ends at the moment the radio is warm and the handset is in her hand. The action is initiated but not completed; that is the cut.
- The **face-down page**: she reads it and folds it into the notebook. This is the chapter's moment of quiet resolution for that object — what she decided about what was on the page is implied by the fact that she keeps it rather than destroying it. But the drafter should not state this.
- The **final run sequence** should be written with the same patience as every other run — not rushed because it is the last. Elena is deliberate. She does not know how to be anything else.
- **No retrospective emotion** about the runs being over. No "this is the last time she would." The prose does not editorialize. If there is weight in the last run, it is in the physical details and the closing of the analyzer's housing, not in the narration's commentary on it.

---

## Continuity Notes

- Tape dropout: **23 seconds** (Run 6, Day 12). This is the final measurement; the core signature is intact. All subsequent chapter references to the tape's state must use this figure.
- Instrument margin: **0** after this chapter. No further protocol runs are possible.
- Power reserve: **~3 %** — at life-support threshold. The generator will sustain the hab heating and lights through the team's arrival at 1300, but there is no further margin for instrument draws.
- The **evidence package** is now assembled in the main hab: tape housing, wrapped printout, analysis notebook (with the folded page inside), protocol folder (Runs 1–6 logs), photographic film (twelve frames, undeveloped).
- The **face-down page** has been folded into the analysis notebook. Its content remains undisclosed until and unless Chapter 15 implies it.
- The new voltage regulator component arrives with Walczak on Day 12 and will allow the generator to be repaired — but this is past the chapter's events.

# Chapter 15 — The Plane

**One-line summary:** The LC-130 lands; the team arrives; Elena brings Walczak to the equipment building and opens her analysis notebook; the chapter closes before he finishes reading.

**POV:** Dr. Elena Hartmann  
**Tense:** Third-person limited past  
**Setting:** Winslow Station — exterior (arrival strip), main hab, equipment building. Day 12, ~1300.  
**Target words:** ~1,900  
**Chapter shape:** Multi-scene — arrival sequence, then interior encounter with the team  
**Ending mode:** Elliptical

---

## Escalation (from Chapter Map)

- **(a) Day 12, arrival**
- **(b)** Days to foreclosure: **0** — the LC-130 has landed. Power reserve critical (generator near minimum safe output; Walczak will see the power gauge immediately).
- **(c)** **FINAL FORECLOSURE:** the choice is no longer Elena's alone. Whatever she has done with the data, the team knows or will know. The outcome — whether the claim survives peer review, whether Lars's corroboration at Mather is ever properly examined, what the institutional machinery does with what she hands them — is past the chapter's close. **At least one thread remains deliberately unresolved.**

---

## Goal

The final chapter is not a coda. The brief specifies: the team's arrival is the moment the decision's consequences become real in a different register — social, professional, institutional. This chapter is about the crossing of that threshold. It is short because the book does not have more room; the days are done. At least one thread must remain unresolved at the chapter's end.

---

## Obstacle

Six people walking into the station she has held alone for twelve days. The social re-entry is itself the obstacle: five other people's warmth and noise and assumptions and questions pressing into the space that has been hers and the signal's and no one else's. Elena must navigate this without either concealing everything or blurting everything. She does not do either.

---

## Action Beats

**Arrival**

1. 1240. Elena is already outside when she hears the engines — the four-prop drone of the Hercules, distant at first, then coming in from the northwest. She can hear it before she can see it. She stands on the snow in the full cold-weather kit, the way she always stands when a plane is coming in.

2. The LC-130 makes one low pass to check the landing strip — standard operating procedure. The ski-equipped landing gear comes down on the second approach. The aircraft settles onto the snow; the skis leave two shallow parallel tracks. The engines do not stop immediately; they cycle down slowly.

3. The cargo ramp goes down. Walczak is first out, as he always is. He scans the station before he scans Elena — his engineer's eye going to the antenna array, the equipment building, the receiver hut, the hab. Looking for what's wrong. Then he looks at her.

4. He crosses the ice. The others are behind him — four more people, cargo being offloaded. She knows their faces; they are the faces she has not seen for twelve days.

5. "How's the generator?" Walczak says. The first words. He always asks about the machine first; this is not coldness.

6. She tells him: the voltage regulator fault has been active since Day 3. The power reserve is critical — she shows him the percentage. He should install the new component as soon as the equipment is at temperature. She is accurate and complete about the machine.

7. He looks at her more carefully. He does not ask the next question yet — the cargo is coming off the plane and he is tracking four things at once. He says: "Come inside when the cargo's squared away."

**Inside**

8. The hab. Five people in it, plus Elena. The smell of bodies and cold weather gear and the food they have brought from McMurdo. The particular noise of people who have been in a crowd at McMurdo now filling a space that seats six. It is overwhelming in a way that Elena does not fully expect.

9. The others greet her — brief, warm, the practiced ease of people who have been in the field before and know that re-entry is its own kind of weather. She responds to each. She is present enough. Coffee is made; someone brought fresh food from McMurdo; there is the small celebration of supply.

10. Elena watches Walczak across the room. He is doing the equipment building walkthrough he always does when he returns — the systematic check of everything he left behind. She knows he will get to the receiver hut and see the signal analyzer's run log in the protocol folder. She does not know how long she has before that.

11. She gets there first.

**The equipment building**

12. She goes to the equipment building and picks up the evidence package from where she left it — the tape housing, the wrapped printout, the analysis notebook, the protocol folder. She carries it to the equipment building's work table.

13. Walczak comes in. He sees her at the table. He sees the evidence package. He sees the power gauge, which is reading just above its minimum safe line.

14. She opens the analysis notebook. She does not begin with the evidence summary; she begins with Run 1, Day 1. She sets the notebook on the table in front of him and says, in the voice she uses for exactly this kind of communication — patient, precise, without emphasis — "I need you to read this."

15. Walczak sits down. He reads.

16. The chapter does not show what he reads — the reader has been with Elena through all of it; the notebook contains what we know. What we do not know is what it looks like to another person, reading it for the first time.

17. **The chapter ends before Walczak looks up from the notebook.**

---

## Outcome / Elliptical (at least one thread unresolved)

The chapter closes at the moment the data passes from Elena's sole possession into another person's attention. The narrative cuts before Walczak's reaction, before his question, before the institutional chain takes the next step. What Elena has done with the data is now known: she has kept it, she has documented it, and she has given it — all of it, the tape and the printout and the notebook and the protocol runs — to Walczak in the first private moment after the team's arrival.

**The deliberately unresolved thread:** what will the world make of what she has handed him? Whether the claim survives peer review, whether Mather Station's corroborating data is ever properly examined, what happens when the agencies receive the information, whether the second parametric segment can be reconstructed from the tape under controlled conditions — all of this is past the chapter's close and past the novel's reach. The book ends at the moment of transfer, not at the moment of reception.

---

## Craft Notes for the Drafter

- The arrival must be written with the sensory specificity of someone who has been alone for twelve days and is suddenly not: the smell of other people's cold weather gear, the noise of multiple voices, the specific warmth of more bodies in the hab's thermal economy. Elena is not hostile to this; she is simply recalibrating after being alone.
- Walczak's first words ("How's the generator?") are his. They are not emotionally cold — they are the professional vocabulary of someone who knows Elena and knows that asking about the machine is how you ask if everything is okay. The drafter should let the reader feel this without stating it.
- The chapter does **not** describe the signal's content — not in the notebook, not in what Elena says to Walczak, not in any form. She opens to Run 1 and says "I need you to read this." The prose does not render what he reads.
- The **elliptical cut** before Walczak looks up is the novel's last sentence or very nearly so. It must be absolute — the chapter does not add a reflective coda after the cut. The cut is the end.
- The **face-down page** (from Chapter 13) is folded into the notebook; Walczak will encounter it when he reads. Its presence in the notebook without explanation is one element of the deliberately unresolved texture of the ending.

---

## Continuity Notes

- The **tape** (23-second dropout, core signature intact), **printout** (two degraded columns), **analysis notebook** (complete evidence summary, protocol logs, folded page), and **undeveloped film** are all present at the transfer in this chapter.
- The **power reserve** is at ~3 % when Walczak arrives. He will see this immediately; Elena tells him to install the new regulator component as soon as possible. The generator repair will happen on Day 12, but past this chapter's scope.
- The team that lands: Walczak + four others (characters file names these as Walczak plus four unnamed colleagues). Elena knows all of them by face and name; only Walczak needs to be individuated in this chapter.
- **Lars Engström**: his data at Mather is documented in Elena's notebook (she wrote it on Day 9). Walczak will read it. Whether he contacts Lars is past the chapter's close.
- **At least one thread must remain unresolved** (continuity.md §11). The unresolved thread is the signal's fate past the transfer — not Elena's decision, which is resolved by the act of giving the notebook to Walczak, but the signal's trajectory into the world.
- The LC-130 call sign and arrival time (approximately 1300, from Chapter 13) must be consistent.
- **No coda beyond Day 12** (continuity.md §10). The chapter ends on Day 12. The last sentence is on Day 12. There is no afterward.
