# After

The soup had come from a tin she did not remember choosing. She had taken a bowl from the drying rack, found the tin on the shelf above the cooktop, opened it, heated the contents in a small pot, and poured it, and all of these actions had apparently occurred while her attention was on something other than soup, because she could not have said precisely when she had begun to be hungry or when she had decided to do something about it. The galley clock read 16:52.

She ate standing at the counter. Not because there was any particular reason to stand — the table was there, the bench seat was empty — but because she had come to the counter and the soup was there and she had not moved. Sitting was apparently a decision she had not yet arrived at.

Outside, the wind had picked up since morning: a flat, irregular pressure against the hab wall, neither increasing nor decreasing, simply present. The generator ran in the equipment building at its usual pitch. She had been listening to the generator for eleven weeks, and what she heard now was the usual pitch. The standby light on the SSB radio was red and steady.

She finished the soup. Set the bowl in the sink. Stood for a moment at the counter with her hands on the edge, not thinking in any directed way — not reviewing the morning, not drawing a conclusion from it, not doing what she would normally do at the end of a significant event. The significant event had passed. What remained was the particular state of being present in the afternoon of the day it had passed, which turned out to have its own quality, different from anticipation and different from aftermath and not quite either.

Outside the hab windows, the dark.

---

Then the tone from the equipment building.

Low-register, below the threshold at which it could be called a sound without qualification — more like a change in the quality of the generator's output than a sound distinct from it. She had heard it twice before: once in April, once in the second week of May. Both times the tone had persisted for thirty to forty seconds and resolved on its own. She had logged both events.

This one did not resolve.

She went.

The equipment building was four degrees colder than the hab, its heater drawing from the same generator whose fault was now active. The output display read 89%, the needle moving in a slow irregular arc between 88 and 91. The voltage regulator fault light was amber. Not red: amber was monitored deviation, not instrument emergency. She had looked up the distinction in the third week of winter and had retained it without further reference.

She checked the load indicators in sequence: hab base circuit, equipment building, receiver hut. The receiver hut heater was the highest-draw single circuit. She confirmed this against the load schedule on the wall above the panel — a laminated card she had made in March for this winter's operating conditions, circuits listed in order of draw — and then shed the receiver hut heater.

The load indicator dropped. The output gauge steadied at 93%, still in fault range but no longer fluctuating. The fault light remained amber. She sat down on the bench along the west wall and settled in to wait.

Forty minutes. This was the stabilization procedure: reduce load, give the generator time to normalize at the lower draw, then restore. Forty minutes was the minimum interval. She had done this twice and read it in the manual many more times than twice, and the procedure was correct, and what it required of her right now was to sit on the bench and not do anything to the load until the interval had elapsed.

The generator held at 93%. She watched the gauge and listened to it.

What she did not think about was the window. That was not suppression; the window was simply past, the same way April was past and October was past, and thinking about what had already become fixed was a use of attention that she did not have a way to make productive. What occupied the particular attention available to a person sitting on a bench with an instrument fault to monitor and forty minutes to spend was the arithmetic of what was left.

Three runs. Five days.

A tape that had been adding approximately one second of dropout per day since the Run 3 measurement, which was itself derived from two data points — enough to establish a rate, not enough to determine whether that rate was linear or accelerating. Her working estimate put the dropout now at eight seconds. If the rate held through Day 12, it would reach thirteen seconds by the time the LC-130 landed. The signal segment's first parametric region had begun at the tape position where the dropout had started; at thirteen seconds of dropout, the leading boundary of the first parametric region would still be within the readable portion of the tape. Whether the core signature was at risk before or after that point was a question she could not resolve from two data points.

Three data points would not resolve it either, but they would constrain it. If she ran on Day 8, Day 10, and Day 12, she would have three additional measurements of the dropout rate and, by the rate's behavior across those intervals, a more defensible estimate of where the core signature stood on Day 12. Tighter bounds on a number that was still growing were not the same as good news. But they were the most she could do, and she had learned not to misidentify the most she could do.

Each run would cost seven percentage points of the power reserve at the clean-run rate. She was at 41% now. Three runs would bring it to 20%, assuming no further fault events, no brownout warm-up cost, no unanticipated draw. Assuming was the wrong word; 20% was a lower bound that depended on conditions she did not fully control.

She was aware of the receiver hut heater being shed. She would need to check the housing temperature when she restored the draw.

The output gauge held at 93%. The fault light was amber, steady.

---

At minute forty-three, she restored the receiver hut heater.

The gauge dipped to 90% and stabilized within thirty seconds. The fault light went dark. She watched it for two minutes, then picked up the log and wrote:

*Day 7 afternoon. Generator fault: voltage regulator active fault. Output: 89%, fluctuating. Stabilization procedure: shed receiver hut heater for 43 min. Post-shed output: stabilized at 93%. On restoration: dipped to 90%, stabilized. Fault light extinguished. No instruments lost.*

She looked at the entry. It recorded what had happened accurately. It did not record that this was the third fault event of the winter, or that the first two had been in April and May and had resolved without intervention, or that this one had not, or that the post-restoration output was 90% rather than the 97% baseline that had been the pre-fault standard. These were observations she could make from the three log entries together; the individual entry was not the place for them. She underlined *No instruments lost* as a matter of habit, because that was the fact with the most consequence, and habit was how she kept herself from deciding which facts had consequence based on how she felt about them in the moment of writing.

She would need to go outside to check the exhaust pipe.

---

The cold-weather kit hung on the rack beside the exterior door: insulated overtrousers, parka, balaclava, goggles, gauntlets. She had been in this kit forty times or more this winter. The sequence for dressing was fixed and she performed it in order — overtrousers first, both legs seated before the waist was secured; parka, zip checked twice; balaclava fitted before the parka collar was sealed; goggles, gasket against the face-surround checked; gauntlets last — not because she was in danger of doing it wrong, but because the sequence was correct and performing a correct sequence incorrectly was a particular kind of waste. She had learned not to rush it. Seven minutes.

She pushed the exterior door open.

The temperature was minus forty-two Celsius. There was no wind at this moment. She was aware of the wind's absence the way she was aware of a gauge reading within normal range: noted, but by the absence of the deviation, not by the presence of the norm. No wind. She went around to the south wall.

The exhaust pipe was clear. No frost accumulation at the terminus, no partial ice at the bend. The pipe was warm enough along its final section that icing had not had the opportunity to begin during the fault and recovery. She confirmed this with the flashlight and straightened.

She looked up.

The sky was not black. That was not the right word for what it was, because black implied the absence of texture, and there was texture — the stars at sixty-eight degrees south in mid-June, with no moon and no aurora, were dense enough to appear as a surface rather than as points on a background. A surface with gradation: brighter toward the galactic center, fainter in the high-declination bands, the faint lateral structure of the plane running across it at an angle that did not correspond to any angle on the ground. She had been outside in this dark enough times this winter to know that the knowledge of it was not adequate preparation for standing under it. You could carry the knowledge and still be stopped by the fact.

She stood for a moment that was longer than exhaust-pipe confirmation required.

---

What she was not going to do: use a relay channel that had closed at 0848.

That option had been present for six days and was no longer present. The decision space she had been working in that morning was not the decision space she was working in now. Eight hours was not enough time to have fully characterized what the new one contained. She had been characterizing it since the bench in the equipment building, between gauge-readings.

What it contained: hand the data and the analysis notebook to Walczak on Day 12, in whatever state the tape was in by then. Destroy the data — not as a direction she was moving toward, but as a door that existed in the same room as the other doors. Pursue some form of publication from here, which would require communication resources and documentation support and a submission window that nothing at Winslow could produce in five days. The third door was nearly flush with the wall. She could see it was there.

And Lars — the thought arrived with the specificity of something she had been carrying since morning without examining. Lars at Mather Station, sixty kilometers east, with a reading in the UHF secondary band that he had filed as artifact and that Elena had confirmed was not an artifact by telling him it probably was. Something there. But there were sixty kilometers between them and a radio protocol that did not permit the conversation the data required, and she did not follow the thought further.

She stood under the stars for another thirty seconds. Then she went back inside.

---

She removed the cold-weather kit in reverse order and hung each piece on its peg. She went to the galley and filled the kettle.

While the kettle heated, she walked the covered walkway to the receiver hut.

The tape housing temperature gauge read minus thirteen point eight Celsius — eight-tenths above the lower threshold. She had expected some temperature drop from the forty-three minutes of heater shed; eight-tenths of a degree drop from the 70% protocol norm was within the range the housing was rated to tolerate. The gauge needle was moving: recovering, at the rate she would have expected from the restored heater draw. She unlatched the housing cover and drew her flashlight across the reel.

The timing marks were where they had been that morning. Binder stress zone leading edge: three to four millimeters inside the signal-boundary mark, consistent with the two-angle reading she had logged at 05:41. Eight seconds. She held the beam at the grazing angle and read the surface. She did not need to recalculate; she had not expected to find it different. She latched the cover.

She checked the power reserve gauge on the receiver hut's auxiliary panel: 38%. Three points down from where the morning had ended, the fault response and the afternoon having spent what they had spent.

She stood for a moment with her hand on the housing's outer surface. The housing was doing what it was rated to do. The tape inside it was doing what degraded tape in the cold did. Both facts were accurate, and both were less good than they had been two days ago, and they would be less good than this two days from now.

She went back to the galley.

---

The kettle was ready. She poured the water and let the tea steep and then she sat down at the table, which was the first time she had sat down that afternoon. The mug was warm against both hands.

The tea cooled. She did not drink it. She did not open the fieldwork notebook, which was on the table's corner where she had left it after the window. She did not go to the fax terminal to look at the send queue. She sat at the table with the cooling mug and the fieldwork notebook closed, and on the SSB console, the red standby light was steady — exactly as it always had been, from the first week of winter to this one, unchanging through everything the intervening weeks had changed.

She had not made a decision. She had made a calculation. The two were different things, and she knew which one she had done.

input.oneLine: Post-gate afternoon: a generator fault forces Elena through the stabilization procedure and outside; she calculates three runs, five days, and a degrading tape, and sits with the arithmetic and no decision made.

input.summary: Day 7, afternoon and evening. Elena makes soup in the galley without sitting down — the mechanical function of a person keeping herself operational in the hours after the window closed. A low-register generator alarm sounds mid-afternoon; she goes to the equipment building and finds the voltage regulator fault light active, output at 89%, fluctuating. She runs the stabilization procedure: identifies the receiver hut heater as the highest-draw circuit, sheds it, waits 43 minutes on the bench. During the wait, she works through the arithmetic of what remains — 3 runs, 5 days, a tape degrading at roughly 1 second per day, projected dropout of 13 seconds by Day 12 if the rate holds. At minute 43 she restores the heater, writes the log entry, and notes the fault light gone dark. She dresses in the full cold-weather kit (7 minutes, correct sequence) and goes outside to check the exhaust pipe: no icing. She stands under the Antarctic winter sky — stars dense enough to appear as a surface, not points — for longer than the check requires. Outside, she rehearses the post-gate decision space: the relay is gone; the remaining exits are hand-to-team, destroy, or publish (the third is nearly flush with the wall). Lars — the thought arrives briefly, precise, and she does not follow it. She returns inside, removes the kit, and goes to the receiver hut: housing temperature at -13.8°C (recovering; 8-tenths below protocol norm), tape visual check confirms 8 seconds at the timing marks (unchanged from morning), power reserve gauge reads 38% (down 3 points from 41%). Back in the galley, she makes tea, sits down for the first time that afternoon, and does not drink it. She does not open the fieldwork notebook. She does not go to the fax terminal. The standby light is red and steady. She has not made a decision. She has made a calculation.

input.content:
# Core Dropout

The voltage output needle had settled into a wider arc than the winter had produced before the fault. Plus or minus seven percent: she had written that figure in the equipment log when she first characterized it this morning, and standing at the panel now with four minutes left on the stabilization timer, the figure was confirmed. The arc completed roughly every twenty-one seconds. It had not narrowed during the fifteen-minute reduced-draw procedure; it would not narrow. What the procedure accomplished was equilibrium at the lower load, not correction of the underlying fault. The fault had been stabilized, not repaired. She had written both terms in the log because the distinction was real and she preferred her records to reflect what they could reflect accurately.

The generator time was 08:21. The timer read 00:03:47.

She had gone to the receiver hut first this morning, before the generator panel, before coffee. The tape inspection constrained everything else; that was the correct order. The housing temperature gauge had read minus fourteen point two Celsius — within the rated band, marginally below the 70% protocol norm but within the measurement uncertainty of a non-laboratory field thermometer. She had accepted it. She had opened the housing cover and drawn the flashlight across the reel at the two standard angles, and what she had found on the reel was larger than it had been on Day 4.

The binder stress zone along the outer edge of the reel — that graduated region she had been measuring since Run 2, marking its position against the pencil lines on the housing interior, tracking the advance of its leading edge toward the signal segment boundary — had widened. The zone itself: wider along the reel edge. The active gradient at the leading edge: steeper, the two-millimeter transition band she had measured on Day 4 now closer to three. She had updated the measurement card clipped to the housing's back panel. She had noted the change. The leading edge was still in the outer circumference of the reel, still in advance of the monitoring-record / signal-segment boundary mark, exactly as the degradation rate she had been projecting predicted it should be.

She closed the housing and came back down the walkway.

The needle completed its arc. 209 to 224 volts, approximately, at a nominal of 216. This was, by any reasonable definition, too wide. The fault had not been in the winter plan, and the widened variance had not been in the winter plan, and the stabilization procedure she was running to compensate for the widened variance had not been in the winter plan. None of those things changed the fact of the needle, which was doing what the needle was doing regardless of what had been in the plan.

The timer reached 00:00:00.

She moved to the analyzer's main circuit breaker.

---

The warm-up cycle ran for four minutes and twenty-two seconds, the amber numerals stepping through their self-test sequence in the prescribed order: input calibration, frequency reference, parametric filter sweep verification, playback head alignment check. She had timed this cycle in Runs 1 and 3 to confirm it was completing within specification. It was completing within specification. The self-test indicators resolved green in sequence — all of them — and the display settled to standby.

She loaded the tape.

The reel seated correctly in the transport mechanism. Spindle engaged. She ran the manual tension check: the resistance was at the lower end of the normal range, where it had been since Run 2, which she had noted in Run 2's log and again in Run 3's, and which was not, by itself, cause to stop. She initialized the playback at the signal marker — the timestamp annotation she had placed in the run log on the first night, which she had transferred to each subsequent run log in the same position — and moved back to the display.

She stood with the pen in hand, the run log open to a fresh page.

She had been in this position four times now. The first time at 22:49 on the night of June first, when the self-test had completed and the amber numerals had steadied and she had stood at the display not yet knowing whether the run would confirm what she had or invalidate it. She had known by 23:11. She had known each time; that was what a run produced: a number where there had been a question, a resolved state where there had been an open one. That was the mechanism. She was running the mechanism a fourth time.

The tape began to move.

First parametric segment: she watched the display. Silence. The opening region of the segment, where the dropout had been since Run 3 — where she had measured it, estimated it, projected its growth from Day 4 through Day 7 — was silent, as expected. She counted the seconds. Four. Five. Six. Seven. Eight.

The frequency distribution resolved out of the baseline and the parametric profile began to read.

She noted the values as they came through, writing in the log column by column: frequency stability, spectral density, timing parameters, phase relationship across the secondary receiver channels. She wrote quickly but without rushing; the values needed to be legible, not fast. The first parametric profile was coming through cleanly. Frequency stability: consistent with Runs 1–3, within the expected variance range for the instrument and conditions. Spectral density distribution: consistent, the characteristic shape she had first identified on the night of June first, present and unchanged. Timing parameters: matched. Phase relationship: matched.

She kept writing.

The segment ran for what she estimated, by the time counter, as approximately twenty-two seconds from the point at which the silence ended — twenty-two seconds of clean first-parametric-segment data, beginning at the eight-second mark and continuing to the segment's close. The parametric profile described in those twenty-two seconds was internally consistent and matched, in every parameter she could read from the display, the profile she had confirmed three times before.

She noted the segment's end time in the log margin.

The transition followed. She knew this transition: two to three seconds, a structural property of the signal rather than of the tape, a brief gap between the first and second parametric regions that was present because it was a feature of what had been received. She had noted its duration in Run 1's log, confirmed it in Run 2, and confirmed it again in Run 3. Three seconds. She watched it complete.

The transition ended.

She waited for the second parametric segment to begin.

The display showed: baseline. The flat output the analyzer produced when the tape was blank.

She waited. Counted to ten. The baseline continued.

Fifteen seconds.

The baseline continued.

She stopped the run.

---

She rewound to the second segment marker.

Initiated the playback.

The baseline ran. Ran. Ran. At twelve seconds — she was watching the time counter precisely — the display changed. The signal resumed: the calibration tail, the structured end of the event, the final portion of the forty-seven seconds that confirmed the event's total duration. It read cleanly from the twelve-second mark.

She stopped the run. Rewound to the second segment marker.

Same result.

She rewound a third time. Brought the tape back to the marker, started the counter from the beginning of the second segment, initiated the playback, and watched from the start. Twelve seconds of baseline. Then the resumption. Twelve seconds of blank oxide where the second parametric segment should have been.

She did not run it a fourth time.

She let the remainder of the run complete from the twelve-second resumption point: calibration tail, post-event baseline. Both read clearly. The time counter showed the event's total duration: forty-seven seconds. The instrument run counter read 02 when the tape reached the end of the signal section and the playback stopped.

She collected the printout from the output tray and did not look at it yet.

Power reserve: she checked the gauge on the way through the equipment building. Thirty percent. Eight points down from this morning's thirty-eight.

---

She carried the printout to the work chair in the equipment building and sat with it in her lap.

This was the procedure: read the log from the beginning, assuming the error was hers, going through each step in the run sequence, identifying each point at which a mistake might have been introduced, eliminating them in order. This was what she had done with every anomalous result in thirty years of field work, and it was the right approach because the procedure was the mechanism by which she could tell the difference between a real result and an operator error. She had been wrong about results before. She had been careful about this.

Stabilization procedure: completed at the full fifteen-minute interval. Variance at +/-7%, documented and within the range the procedure was designed to address. No fault light active during the stabilization window. No alarm signal.

Warm-up cycle: self-test completed within specification. All self-test indicators green. No instrument fault signal prior to initialization. The voltage variance during warm-up: within the range she had documented.

Tape loading: correct procedure. Reel seated, spindle engaged, tension within the normal range. She had logged the tension reading. No deviation from the procedure at the loading step.

Playback initialization: at the signal marker, the same marker she had used in all prior runs.

First parametric segment: the dropout at seconds 0–8 was consistent with Run 3's confirmed five-second figure and the Day 6 and Day 7 visual estimates of eight seconds. The values from the readable portion of the segment — from second eight forward — matched Runs 1, 2, and 3 within the expected instrument variance.

Transition: duration consistent with prior runs.

Second parametric segment:

She held at the second parametric segment entry in the run log. The log showed: no signal, 0 to 12 seconds. At 12 seconds: signal resumes at calibration tail start position.

She could not construct a procedure error that explained twelve seconds of blank oxide. The stabilization procedure addressed voltage variance in the instrument circuit; it did not affect tape condition. The warm-up cycle addressed instrument calibration; it did not affect tape condition. The tension check addressed the transport mechanism; it did not affect tape condition. A procedure error could explain anomalous values, distorted output, misread frequencies. A procedure error could not produce twelve seconds of blank oxide followed by a clean resumption.

Blank oxide meant the magnetic coating had failed in that region. The signal had been there, recorded by the receiver on the night of June first, and now the surface that had held the recording was gone.

She had not made an error.

She set the run log on the bench and opened the analysis notebook.

---

She opened to a fresh page and wrote at the top: *Run 4 — Day 8.*

She wrote what the run had confirmed.

*First parametric segment (dropout: 0–8s, consistent with Run 3 and Day 6–7 visual estimates):* Frequency distribution, spectral density, timing parameters, and phase relationship consistent with Runs 1–3. Approximately twenty-two seconds of clean data following the dropout onset. Parametric profile intact across all measurable parameters. Primary anomalous parameters: [she wrote them out, three lines of technical notation in the compact form she used for instrument values — eleven entries in two columns, the notation she would use if she were writing a methods section, because it was precise and she did not know a more precise form].

*Third segment (calibration tail):* Intact. Signal duration confirmed: forty-seven seconds.

*Core signature:* The structural characteristics identifying the signal as non-terrestrial and non-natural are present in the first parametric segment and confirmed across four runs.

She wrote what the run had not confirmed.

*Second parametric segment:* Unreadable. Twelve seconds of blank oxide from segment start. Confirmed on three separate playbacks. The binder failure is in the core of the tape record, not at the reel edge. The second parametric segment extends the parametric profile and provides the data required to distinguish between the three alternative classifications the verification protocol was designed to rule out. This segment is not recoverable from this tape by any means available at this station.

She read the entry from the top.

Each sentence was accurate. She confirmed this one sentence at a time, the same way she had gone through the run log.

Then she wrote the accounting.

*What the remaining evidence supports:* The signal was received. Its duration was forty-seven seconds. It was received in the upper UHF monitoring band at 22:21:52 on 1 June 1991 at Winslow Station. The primary anomalous parameters of the first parametric segment are [reference: entries above]. These parameters, considered together, characterize the signal as non-terrestrial and non-natural by the criteria of the verification protocol. This characterization has been confirmed across four instrument runs. A provisional claim on this basis is supportable.

*What the remaining evidence does not support:* The complete parametric characterization the verification protocol was designed to establish — the determination that would exclude all three alternative classifications and allow the finding to be rated as confirmed rather than provisional. The second parametric segment is required for that determination. The 1990 revision to the protocol made this requirement explicit, and the requirement was correct; the first segment alone is insufficient to close the three alternative classifications. The second parametric segment is gone.

She set the pen down on the notebook's spine.

The word *gone* was the right word. She had arrived at it without deliberation and she confirmed it now by reading the sentence. The second parametric segment was gone. It was not degraded; it was not partially readable; it was not accessible by a method she had not yet tried. It was blank oxide. She had played it three times and would get the same result on a fourth, fifth, or sixth play.

The 1990 revision to the protocol had added the second segment's requirement because she had calculated, in 1990, that the first segment alone was insufficient. She had been right in that calculation. The first segment's data — what remained of it, the twenty-two seconds after the dropout — described the signal's primary anomalous parameters precisely and without ambiguity. Those parameters were real. They characterized a real event. A provisional claim built on those parameters was a real claim.

It was not the claim the protocol had been designed to produce.

---

She closed the analysis notebook and carried the run log printout back to the receiver hut.

The protocol folder was on the shelf above the work table: manila, binder-clipped, holding four run log printouts now, plus the initial detection documentation and the three pages of instrument verification notes from the first week. She filed Run 4 behind Run 3. Returned the folder to the shelf.

She stood at the work table.

The tape was in its housing. The signal analyzer was in standby, amber numerals showing the output counter at 02. The heater ran at seventy percent. The housing temperature gauge, from the angle she was standing, read minus fourteen point one.

She had been tracking the binder stress zone along the reel edge for eight days. She had measured it on Day 2, Day 4, Day 6, Day 7, and today. She had projected its advance toward the signal segment boundary and estimated the rate of dropout growth in the first parametric segment from the same data. The measurements had been at the edge because the degradation had been at the edge. She had been watching the right location for the source of the problem she could see.

The second parametric segment was not at the edge.

She stood with the folder for a moment longer, then set it back on the shelf. She put on the outer layer from the hook beside the door and walked back through the walkway to the main hab.

# Sixty Kilometers East

She was writing the morning variance figure when she noticed how little space remained in the column.

The maintenance log was a commercial scientific format — columns pre-printed in millimeter increments, four pages per week, the same size she had been using in field conditions for thirty years because it was the correct size. The voltage variance column had nine entries now, one per day since the winter's first morning check, and when she opened the log to add the Day 9 reading she could see that perhaps three or four lines remained before the column would run out and she would continue in the margin.

She wrote the figure: **+/- 8%.** She drew the direction arrow: **↑.**

The needle was wider in its arc than yesterday. She had timed three cycles before writing the figure — the arc ran approximately twenty-two seconds per cycle at the current load — and the extremes had settled at 209 and 227 against the nominal 218 volts. Plus or minus nine and a half volts. At 218 nominal, that was eight and a half percent, rounded to eight in the log because she was working from visual observation and false precision was worse than the appropriate rounding.

Plus or minus eight. One percentage point wider than the figure she had written in the same column yesterday.

She moved to the secondary gauges. Power reserve: twenty-six percent. Four points down from the thirty she had logged at the end of Run 4 — overnight passive draw, consistent with the established rate for the current operating conditions. She wrote it in the reserve column and left the direction arrow off; the direction was not in question.

Then she ran the arithmetic at the panel, because the panel was where it needed to be done. Each remaining protocol run required a fifteen-minute stabilization procedure before initiation, designed to hold the voltage variance inside the analyzer's safe operating range during the draw. The procedure cost three to four percentage points of reserve above the run itself — she had measured this on Run 4. Three to four points of stabilization plus eight points of baseline run cost: call it eleven to twelve per run total.

At twenty-six percent: two runs, at eleven to twelve points each, left a floor of two to four points. That was the margin. Two runs, barely, if the variance did not widen further, if no brownout occurred during a run and triggered a warm-up cycle.

She had done this arithmetic yesterday with the previous day's figures. The result had been the same: barely. The variance was one percentage point wider today, which had tightened the barely without changing its name.

She closed the log and set it on the panel shelf. No instrument run this morning. The Lars contact was scheduled at 1400, and spending a run before the contact would be committing a resource to an outcome she hadn't confirmed she needed. She went through the remaining readings in the order she had established: fuel gauge (43.8 liters, consistent with the 5.2-liter-per-day burn rate), heating circuit draw (within the 70% protocol range), receiver hut building monitor (operational, no alarm). She recorded each reading and left the instrument margin column blank.

---

The receiver hut was minus 14.1 when she pushed through the door, the heater running at seventy percent and the instrument rack in standby and the amber numerals on the signal analyzer steady in the standby mode they had been in since Run 4 yesterday. She unclipped the tape housing, opened the cover, and took the flashlight from the work table.

Two standard angles. First angle at the leading edge of the binder stress zone; second angle across the zone's widest extent along the reel edge. The zone had progressed — she could see it, the gradient slightly wider at the leading edge, the zone's overall extent along the reel edge more visible against the clean oxide on either side. She updated the housing inspection card: *Day 9, visual check, zone larger than Day 8, consistent with established progression rate.* 

She did not write a dropout figure. The last instrument-confirmed figure was Run 4's confirmed eight-second dropout in the first parametric segment. Without a run today she had no number beyond the visual estimate, and the visual estimate was of the stress zone's physical extent, not the dropout's acoustic duration. A layer of inference she did not trust enough to record as measurement. The inspection card notation meant she had a direction but not a number, and in her protocol a direction without a number was a provisional assessment.

She filed the provisional assessment and went back up the walkway.

---

In the equipment building she opened the field reference binder to the antenna orientation notes from the setup week in March. The sky region she had been monitoring on the night of June first: azimuth and elevation fixed in the protocol, right ascension and declination of the field center entered in two columns during setup, the bearing from Winslow to the field's center at the relevant hour derivable from those coordinates and the time of observation.

She had looked at these notes before — in the days after Day 1, when she had been trying to determine whether the sky region she was monitoring was in any geometric relation to the location of Mather Station. The bearing was consistent. She confirmed this again now, checking her entry against the orientation notes, then checking the compass bearing to Mather Station against the geographic reference entries someone had written into the binder during a previous season.

Without Lars's precise timestamp, his antenna geometry, his calibration state on June first, and the raw log trace from his secondary background channel, she could not turn bearing consistency into a calculation. What she had was a direction from Winslow to the monitored sky region, a direction from Winslow to Mather Station sixty kilometers east, and the fact that these two directions were not in contradiction. She had known this since Day 2. She could still not do more with it than she could do then.

She closed the binder and set it back on the shelf.

She made coffee, sat at the work table, and did not open the analysis notebook or the contact log or any document that required something added to it. She had spent nine days in this equipment building and she was practiced at waiting without turning the waiting into an occasion. The generator ran at its current load and the voltage needle completed its arcs, twenty-two seconds each, in the rhythm she could time without looking. Outside the small windows of the equipment building: the Antarctic dark, complete and consistent, minus thirty-eight on the exterior sensor.

The time was 11:22.

The contact window would open at 1400.

---

At 1354 she sat at the SSB console and clicked the frequency live.

"Winslow Station, Winslow Station. This is Mather Station. Do you copy."

Lars Engström's voice through the speaker: five by four, the same quality it had been on every contact. She gave him Winslow's report.

Weather first. His wind event had cleared forty-eight hours ago — pressure 29.9 and holding, surface drift light, antenna systems stable since the gusts passed. His overnight low: minus thirty-six. She gave him hers: stable, minus thirty-eight, no precipitation, barometric pressure 29.8 and rising.

He gave her his week's science summary. The atmospheric chemistry results had been within baseline predictions across all monitored compounds. His week-fourteen extraction was complete and the initial mass spectrometer read had come in consistent with the six weeks of baseline preceding it. Equipment calibration holding. Four weeks remaining on his winterover schedule; he expected to reach his program targets. He said it had been a productive season by the data, if a quiet one.

She told him about the generator: Day 7 fault, amber regulator light, variance widened to eight percent now, stabilization procedure required before each remaining instrument run, replacement component arriving on the twelfth. He asked: main unit or backup? Main unit. Did she have what she needed to manage the remaining days? She said she had two runs remaining and would manage them carefully. He said he was sorry the fault had come when it had.

There was a pause in the traffic. The SSB carrier held steady.

Lars said: "I've been going through the instrument logs this week for the monthly report. I wanted to follow up on something I mentioned a few weeks ago."

She had the contact log open and the pen in her hand. "All right," she said.

"The anomalous reading in the UHF secondary band. The report requires me to formally document or formally discard anomalous readings, so I went back to it and timed it from the log trace." On Day 3 he had said: about a minute, perhaps slightly less. She had been working with that timing window since. "I want to give you more precise parameters."

"Go ahead," she said.

"Duration: forty-seven seconds." He said it without emphasis, the same way he said every technical figure. "I should qualify that. The logging interval on the secondary background channel is two seconds, so there's inherent timing uncertainty. I'm stating it as forty-six to forty-eight seconds, center value forty-seven. That's the best estimate the log trace gives me."

She said: "Repeat the duration."

A brief pause — the radio pause of someone confirming they had heard the request correctly. Then Lars repeated it: "Forty-seven seconds. Forty-six to forty-eight, center forty-seven. Two-second logging resolution."

She wrote in the contact log: *47s.* She kept the pen on the page. "Continue," she said.

"Frequency: 432.275 megahertz. The secondary background logger is a passive reference system — it runs continuously, not targeted at any program band. The shift-review software flags events above a threshold at shift end; that's how this reading came to my attention." The detection method she had known from Day 3. The frequency she had not had. "Timestamp: approximately 2208 local on June first. I've cross-checked against adjacent entries in the primary data record. I'm confident in a two-minute window centered on 2208, within the logging interval resolution."

She looked at the contact log. She looked at what she had written: *47s. 432.275 MHz. 2208 June 1.*

She had received her signal at 22:21:52.

"Has this been entered in your formal station log?" she said.

"As an unresolved instrument artifact. I ran full diagnostics on the secondary background system — no equipment fault found. The timing was consistent with a maintenance cycle we ran that week, which is my working attribution. I'll note it in the monthly report as unresolved anomaly, insufficient data for definitive classification."

She said: "What frequency exactly."

He gave it again. She wrote it again, below the first entry, the same pen pressure she used for generator readings and fuel figures: **432.275 MHz.**

"I had something similar here," she said. "I think you're right about RFI."

"Good to know it's not just us," Lars said. "Strange month."

Standard traffic close. Call signs exchanged, signal quality confirmed, formal sign-off. She wrote the contact end time: 1421. She set the handset in the cradle.

She did not move the hand from the cradle for a moment. Then she moved it toward the transmit key and held it near the key without pressing it. Then she moved it back to the table.

She clicked off the carrier. The standby light went from green to red, as it always did.

---

What Lars had in his secondary background channel: a forty-seven-second event at 432.275 megahertz, timestamped approximately 2208 on June first, detected by a passive monitoring system running continuously through the winter, attributed provisionally to local RFI from a maintenance cycle, filed as unresolved artifact in the formal station log, documented for the monthly report as unresolved anomaly, insufficient data for definitive classification.

She had received a forty-seven-second signal at 22:21:52.

Thirteen minutes and fifty-two seconds between those two timestamps. Within Lars's stated two-minute precision window, and within her own instrument's precision.

Mather Station was sixty kilometers east on a bearing she had checked against the field reference binder this morning and confirmed was consistent with the direction of the sky region she had been monitoring on June first. A signal received first at the station further east, at a different frequency band on a different instrument in a different electronics chain, fourteen minutes before the station sixty kilometers to the west received it on a primary monitoring instrument in the upper UHF band: the geometry was consistent with a directed signal from a source bearing east, the beam's arrival at each station a function of that station's position. She had not run the geometry; she could not run it without Lars's raw log trace and his antenna geometry, and she did not have those. But the geometry did not contradict her.

Not proof. Consistent. Two stations. Two instruments. Two frequency bands. Two independent detection events, fourteen minutes apart, sixty kilometers of Antarctic ice sheet between them.

She went to the work table and opened the fieldwork notebook to the analysis section.

She turned to the page after the Run 4 entry and wrote at the top of the fresh page:

*Mather Station (L. Engström). 47s event. 432.275 MHz, UHF secondary, passive background logger. Timestamp approx. 2208 local June 1. T-14 min relative to Winslow detection (22:21:52).*

*Filed: unresolved instrument artifact, Mather station log. Attribution (Engström): possible RFI from maintenance cycle. No equipment fault on diagnostics.*

*Geometry: Mather 60 km east. Bearing consistent with monitored sky region. 14-minute offset consistent with common source, directed signal. Not verified. Raw log data inaccessible.*

She looked at the last line and added: *Status: inaccessible without disclosure.*

She read the entry sentence by sentence.

The SSB console was six feet away. The frequency dial was still set to the contact frequency. The carrier was off; she could switch it live in a moment and reach Mather Station before the contact window closed.

She could say: *Lars, I need the raw log trace for the secondary background channel, June first, 2200 to 2230.* He would ask why. She had said, not fifteen minutes ago, that she thought he was right about RFI. A request for the raw log trace was not consistent with someone who thought they were looking at RFI, and Lars would hear this the way he heard everything on the frequency — not with suspicion, but with the precise attention of a scientist working alone in the dark who had learned to parse radio traffic carefully because everything that mattered came through it.

He would ask why. She would have to answer.

Nine days of not answering.

She looked at what she had written in the contact log: *I had something similar here. I think you're right about RFI.* She had said it in the contact register. The same register she used for the barometric pressure and the heating circuit draw and the contact end time. Lars had heard it and moved to the traffic close, because there was nothing in that register to suggest he should not.

She could not un-say it. She could only say something after it that would require explaining the thing before it, which would require explaining everything before that.

She did not go to the console.

She took the contact log page and folded it once and placed it inside the back cover of the fieldwork notebook, behind the housing inspection card. She closed the notebook.

Three days to foreclosure. She knew the number without writing it.

She walked through the equipment building and out the far door into the main hab corridor, and the door sealed behind her with the sound it always had, which was the same sound it had made on every day of the nine days she had been here alone, and the number at the bottom of what she had not done was three.

She does the stabilization-plus-run arithmetic at the panel — eleven to twelve percent per run now, two runs at that rate leaving a floor of two to four points — and decides not to run the protocol today. She notes the maintenance log column is nearly full. In the receiver hut she does a visual tape inspection, finds the binder stress zone larger than Day 8 but cannot commit a dropout figure without an instrument run. She checks the field reference binder for the bearing from Winslow to her monitored sky region on June first, confirms it's consistent with the bearing to Mather Station, and sets the binder aside — she still cannot complete the geometry calculation without Lars's precise parameters. At 1354 she opens the SSB contact. Standard weather and science exchange. Then Lars says he went back to the anomalous reading for his monthly report. He gives the precise parameters: forty-seven seconds (center of forty-six to forty-eight, limited by two-second logging resolution), 432.275 MHz on the UHF secondary background logger, timestamp approximately 2208 local June first. Elena asks him to repeat the duration; he does. She calculates: 2208 versus her 22:21:52 is fourteen minutes. Mather is sixty kilometers east, bearing consistent with the monitored sky region. Geometry is consistent with a directed signal received first at the more easterly station. Lars says he's filed it as unresolved instrument artifact, attribution to possible RFI from a maintenance cycle. Elena asks for the frequency again, writes it a second time. Then: 'I had something similar here. I think you're right about RFI.' Lars: 'Good to know it's not just us. Strange month.' Signs off. After the radio goes quiet, Elena sits with the handset and does not reach for the key. She writes Lars's parameters into the analysis notebook in the entry format she uses for protocol data: Mather Station, 47s, 432.275 MHz, T-14 min relative to Winslow detection, filed as artifact, geometry consistent, raw data inaccessible. She adds the final notation: 'Status: inaccessible without disclosure.' She could call back; she does not. She folds the contact log page into the notebook's back cover and closes it. Three days to foreclosure.

# The Physical Record

She unrolled the printout on the galley table and weighted the corners — condensed milk tin, tool kit, field reference binder, protocol folder — then positioned the work light to fall across the paper's full width from the left. The thermal blanket went over the back of the chair. She took the laminated examination card from the protocol folder's side pocket and placed it to the left of the printout.

Fourteen columns. The examination card listed them in the order the signal analyzer produced them: frequency, amplitude, time of reception, phase, polarization, signal-to-noise, calibration reference, and seven derived parameter columns from the analyzer's processing. She had printed the card from the original template during the setup week in March, as she had done at the start of every winterover season in which this protocol had been active. She confirmed the column order against the printout's header row and began.

Column 1 was frequency. She ran the two-pass method: first pass down through all twenty-three data rows, checking legibility and completeness; second pass on the eight rows she had marked on the examination card as carrying the signal's peak values. Both passes returned the same result. Column 1 was intact.

Column 2 was amplitude. The same method, the same result. She wrote in the working pad: *Col 1, Col 2: intact.* The signal's frequency and amplitude values were there, all twenty-three rows, all eight flagged rows. She moved to column 3.

Column 3 was the timestamp column: time of reception in UTC, to the hundredth of a second, one entry per acquisition row. Without it, the printout was a document containing measured values with no independently verifiable record of when those values had been acquired. The timestamp was the printout's link to the antenna log in the equipment building's document cabinet, to the station's master clock, to the formal chain that allowed a reader who had not been present to verify that the data had been produced by this instrument, at this station, at the time and under the conditions the protocol required. The timestamp column did not record the signal. It recorded the claim that the recording was legitimate.

At row 4, she stopped.

The ink along the printed numerals showed a fracture pattern — hairline cracks running perpendicular to the direction of print. This was the failure mode thermal paper produced when a substrate contracted in sustained cold: the ink surface, slightly less flexible than the paper beneath it, fractured along its weakest lines rather than flexing. She had documented this pattern in the protocol's failure-mode appendix after seeing similar damage on printout returns from earlier Antarctic deployments, in conditions less extreme than Winslow in June. The row 4 timestamp was partially legible. The first two characters — the hour and minute digits — were intact. Three characters were interrupted by the fracture lines, their correct values inferrable from the progression of adjacent rows, the timestamps incrementing at a consistent interval. The sixth character was absent: the ink had separated from the substrate along the fracture line and taken that position with it.

*Col 3, row 4: partially degraded. Characters 3–5 fractured, recoverable by context. Character 6 absent.*

Row 5 and row 6 were clean. At row 7 the fracture pattern returned, broader. The cracking at row 7 ran across a wider portion of the cell, with the same perpendicular orientation but more extensive surface area — possibly because that row's position fell on a stress line in the paper, a structural differential the cold had amplified over nineteen days of the printout's storage in the equipment cabinet. The row 7 timestamp was legible in roughly half its characters. The remaining half were interrupted at positions where adjacent context did not uniquely constrain the correct digit; the timestamp sequence incremented from row to row in a way that bounded but did not determine what the fractured characters should be.

*Col 3, row 7: partially degraded. Approximately 50% of characters legible. Remaining characters not recoverable.*

At row 12, there was no ink.

She moved the work light to a low oblique angle — the method for detecting the reflectivity differential between intact ink surface and bare paper substrate — and looked at the row 12 position. The paper was structurally present and in its correct sequence location. What had been printed on its surface on the night of June first was not there. The thermal base material caught the oblique light cleanly: smooth, off-white, without printed characters or fracture residue or even the partial texture that remained when ink cracked but did not fully lift. The ink at row 12 of the timestamp column had separated from the substrate entirely and was gone.

*Col 3, row 12: blank. Ink absent.*

She confirmed rows 13 through 23 in the two-pass method and found them intact. Then she moved through columns 4, 5, and 6 — phase, polarization, signal-to-noise — in fourteen minutes and found no degradation in any of the sixty-nine cells she examined.

Column 7 was the calibration reference column. The signal analyzer recorded its calibration state at each acquisition interval: the internal reference oscillator reading, the measured noise floor, and three additional calibration parameters that together described the instrument's operating condition at the moment of measurement. These values did not measure the signal. They recorded the conditions under which the signal was measured — the reference frame against which the raw signal data was calibrated. A reader who wished to verify the accuracy of the measurements in the adjacent columns, rather than accepting the analyzer's own self-assessment of its output, needed column 7's reference values to calculate the calibration corrections the protocol specified. The calibration column was not optional verification; it was what made verification possible.

Row 2 of column 7: hairline fractures, the same pattern as column 3 row 4. She held the loupe over the damaged area and examined each character position in sequence. The reference oscillator value was legible, as was one of the three additional calibration parameters. The noise floor figure and the remaining two additional parameters were interrupted by the fracture lines at positions that were not recoverable from adjacent context.

*Col 7, row 2: partially degraded. Reference oscillator and one additional parameter legible. Noise floor and two additional parameters interrupted.*

Row 9: more extensive damage, and a different character. The fracturing ran diagonally as well as perpendicular to the print direction, indicating contraction stress along more than one axis — a pattern she associated with printouts that had experienced temperature cycling as well as sustained cold. Under the loupe the cracking showed a mosaic structure: separated tiles of ink surface, the gaps between them exposing the paper, the tiles themselves carrying fragments of characters that were no longer connected to one another. She examined the row for two minutes. The values were not recoverable.

*Col 7, row 9: extensively degraded. Multi-directional fracturing. Values not recoverable.*

Columns 8 through 14: she spent thirty-four minutes on these seven columns in the two-pass method, checking each row and the flagged rows for the signal's anomalous parameters. All intact. The frequency distribution across the signal's forty-seven-second duration, the amplitude profile, the phase structure, the polarization state, the signal-to-noise progression, and the seven derived parameter values from the analyzer's processing — legible in all twenty-three rows of all seven columns.

She put the pen down.

The core of what the printout showed was present. The damage was not in the signal's characteristics. It was in the columns that placed those characteristics in a verifiable chain: the timestamp connecting the printout to external records, the calibration reference certifying the measurement conditions under which the data had been produced. The printout's capacity to independently certify its own provenance — to stand alone as a document, without requiring access to the antenna log and the instrument log in the equipment building — was diminished. What remained was the signal's measured parameters, and the documentation that the measured parameters were damaged.

She transferred the working pad notes to the analysis notebook:

*Day 10. Printout examination. Column 3 (timestamp): rows 4, 7 partially degraded; row 12 blank. Column 7 (cal ref): rows 2, 9 degraded. Columns 1, 2, 4–6, 8–14: intact.*

She read the entry, confirmed it against the working pad, and set the pen in the notebook's spine.

---

The station camera was in the field documentation kit on the second shelf of the equipment building — a 35mm SLR, the standard field documentation model, used in March for the antenna alignment record and the receiver rack configuration photographs. She retrieved it from the kit, confirmed the frame counter through the small indicator window: eighteen exposures remaining on the current roll.

She carried the camera back to the galley and positioned it above the printout at sixty centimeters, the 50mm lens on manual focus at the standard documentation distance. The focus ring moved smoothly enough, but the aperture ring required firm pressure — the cold had stiffened the detents, the mechanism functioning correctly at reduced tolerance. She set the aperture, confirmed the exposure through the viewfinder, and began.

First pass: the full length of the printout in overlapping frames, left to right, covering each section with enough lateral overlap that no column fell entirely at a frame edge. She advanced the film between exposures with the winding lever. The lever had developed resistance since March — the lubricant thickened, the mechanism operating correctly but less fluidly than it had during the setup week, when the equipment building had been above minus fifteen and the machinery had moved with more willingness. She advanced each frame with steady, deliberate pressure, feeling the ratchet engage and complete before moving the camera.

Second pass: close range on the damaged columns. She adjusted the focus to forty centimeters and photographed column 3 in two frames — one covering the row 4 and row 7 positions in sequence, one placed on the blank space at row 12, where the oblique light made the absence most visible against the intact rows above and below. Then column 7 in two frames, both focused on the damaged rows.

She checked the counter: twelve exposures used, six remaining.

What the twelve frames on the roll documented was the printout as it existed this morning. When the roll was developed — McMurdo, after the team arrived on Day 12, the first opportunity — the photographs would show the intact columns and the damage in columns 3 and 7: the fracture patterns in the cells she had examined, the interrupted characters, the blank space at row 12 where the oblique light showed nothing but paper. The photographs would confirm that the damage existed and establish its approximate extent.

They would not supply the missing values. A photograph of an absent character showed the absence. A photograph of a fractured cell showed the fracture and the fragments that remained, not the value the fragments had composed before the ink separated. The photographs were a record of what the printout had become, not a record of what it had originally contained. Both were true; they were not equivalent. She had done the documentation available to her, which was what there was to do.

She rewound the roll and noted the camera's state on the working pad — *Roll F: 12 frames used, 6 remaining. No darkroom at Winslow. McMurdo on arrival.* — and returned the camera to the documentation kit.

---

The walkway to the receiver hut was thirty-one paces. The hut was minus fourteen-point-three when she opened the door, the space heater at its standard draw, the signal analyzer in standby with its amber numerals steady in the dim.

She was not going to run the protocol today.

The power reserve was approximately 22 percent by the morning gauge reading — the overnight passive draw had pulled it down two points from the previous evening's estimate. Each remaining instrument run required the fifteen-minute stabilization procedure, designed to hold the voltage variance inside the analyzer's safe operating range during the draw. At the current variance of plus or minus eight percent, the procedure cost three to four points of the reserve before the run began. Eight points for the run itself at baseline rate. Eleven to twelve total. Two runs remaining: one for Day 11, one for Day 12. The floor after both, if the variance held and no brownout added to the cost, would be somewhere between two and four percent. The range was not generous enough to commit one of the remaining runs on a day when conditions were not optimal.

This was not an optimal day. She was measuring.

She unclipped the tape housing from the rack and opened the cover, then positioned the flashlight at the standard first angle for the housing inspection.

The binder failure zone was visible at once — the band of lighter-colored surface where the magnetic binder had separated from the polyester substrate, the base film exposed in a strip against the darker oxide on each side. She had been measuring this zone's extent since the first confirmed dropout on Run 3, Day 4, using the timing marks printed on the housing's internal frame: two-second intervals, indexed to the reel's angular position. She located the failure zone's leading edge, measured its position relative to the nearest timing mark, and calculated the offset. Then she moved the flashlight to the second standard angle — the oblique position that sharpened the boundary between failed and intact oxide — and measured again.

Eighteen seconds.

Both measurements agreed within half a mark.

She held the housing at the work table for a moment. Then she opened the housing inspection card and wrote: *Day 10, visual est., 18s. Zone wider than Day 8. Leading edge approaching boundary of first segment core region.*

The progression she had been logging: five seconds confirmed on Run 3, Day 4. Eight seconds estimated by visual inspection on Days 6 and 7. Twelve seconds confirmed on Run 4, Day 8. Eighteen seconds now, estimated by the same visual method.

The intervals between successive measurements: three seconds in two days, then four seconds in two days, then six seconds in two days. The most recent interval was the largest yet. She used it as the working rate — three seconds per day — because it was the most recent data point and because underestimating the rate was the error she could not afford to make. At that rate, the failure zone's leading edge would reach the boundary of the first parametric segment's core signature region in approximately two to three days.

The core signature was intact. She had confirmed this on Run 4 and had not been able to confirm it since, because confirming it required a protocol run and she had budgeted the remaining runs for tomorrow and the day after. What she had today was a visual estimate and the arithmetic derived from it. The arithmetic said two to three days. Run 5 tomorrow would give her the instrument measurement.

She clipped the housing back in the rack and filed the inspection card.

---

She rewrapped the printout in the thermal blanket when she returned to the hab — both ends folded, the roll placed back in the equipment cabinet with the same careful grip she had used to carry it to the table that morning. She stood for a moment at the open cabinet, looking at the wrapped roll on the shelf. Then she closed the cabinet.

She transferred the Day 10 log entry from the working pad to the station log:

*Day 10. Printout: Col 3, Col 7 partial degradation (see examination record). Photographs: 12 frames, Roll F. Tape: visual dropout estimate 18s. No instrument run. Power reserve estimate 20%.*

She read the entry and confirmed each item. Then she closed the log.

She did not make tea. There was a period at this hour when a task block ended and the next one had not yet begun, and she usually made tea in that period. She left the kettle on the shelf. She went and sat in the chair beside the work table.

The hab held the quiet it had held for ten days: the heating circuit at its base draw, the generator's load-hum from the equipment building, the periodic tick of the corridor hatch contracting in the cold. The hatch seal was cracked at its lower corner — she had noted it in the first week — and the sound it made when the metal moved was a small, irregular interval she had stopped registering as a sound and had started registering as time passing.

The analysis notebook was closed in front of her on the table. She did not open it.

Across the room the SSB radio's standby light was red on the console, throwing its small disk of color on the wall. The disk sat at the angle it always held against that wall. The light was what it had been on the first night in this hab, the same red, the same position, and the physical record of the signal it did not know about was smaller tonight than it had been that night and smaller than it would be tomorrow night.

She sat with that and did not reach for the handset.
